reviewText: First, let me say that I am an avid Kindle user and have been from the days of Kindle 1. Over the years since the first Kindle, I have purchased vast quantities of Kindle books. Currently, I own 5 Kindles (6 with the Fire HD). They are: the Kindle 1 (by far the best display of all the later e-ink kindles with an SD card slot and a user replaceable battery, which later editions omitted), returned a Kindle 2 for display issues, kept a Kindle 3 (Keyboard), own 2 Kindle touches, the original Fire, and now the Fire HD. All are used by my family. So when I ordered the KF-HD it was with high expectations of really wanting to love this thing. I use the original Fire all the time and love it. Here's what I found about the new Kindle Fire HD:Out of the box the hardware is impressive to say the least, and having used it extensively since receiving it, I find it this Kindle has too many problems to justify keeping the unit until they fix some MAJOR engineering mistakes and software inadequacies that are embarrassingly idiotic. The first Kindle Fire works great. This one, well, leaves much to be desired. Here are the Pros and Cons, as I have experienced them:Pros:1. Fantastic sound with the Dolby turned on. If this feature is off, the speakers sound worse than the original Kindle Fire. You can get this same sound on the original Kindle Fire using good external speakers or a good set of headphones.2. Whispersync with Voice (concurrent with a very big con, see below).3. Text to Speech.4. Very crisp and clear display (with a concurrent con, see below).Cons:1. The HD video display when viewing videos is either slightly on the orange to green side for skin tones (as compared to the original KF). The original Kindle Fire had much more realistic flesh tones on videos. All videos, at least in my opinion.2. The power cable attaches to the side of the unit, rather than at the top or bottom, making it impossible to charge and watch or read anything in landscape mode while charging. This is a major inconvenience. Given a choice between an HDMI cable output and a charging indicator, give me a charging indicator and let the Cloud do its job so it's unnecessary to plug in the Fire to a TV.3. No charging indicator light. How basic is this?? All other Kindle's have indicator lights! Was this an oversight? Or,engineering stupidity at it's best...you decide.4. Power switch and volume control are flush with the casing, impossible to see and/or find in the dark-unless you turn the unit on its side and push til you find a switch.5. Consistently has problems connecting with a wireless connection, giving the error of "authentication failure", making it necessary to connect using the "Settings, Wireless, Connect" from the settings menu (works fine after that).6. Whispersync for Voice and Audible.com do not communicate well at all! I bought several books (free) with free associated audio books from audible.com. What a nightmare! Audible.com does not automatically link your Amazon account, and when it does, it picks the first 3 devices to use on your account there. If the first 3 do not list your kindle fire HD, you cannot download the books wirelessly to your device from Amazon's Manage Your Kindle page or Audible.com's My Library page. Further, unless you deregister your device and then re-register it, you cannot change the order of the availability of your devices. However, when you do download the book and follow the link for "professional narration", it will link in for a purchase. You must then open your book in the Kindle Fire HD, and touch the bottom of the screen on the Chapter 1 page (beginning of book) for it to first download a sample audio, and then the purchased audio from Audible.com. MAJOR HASSLE. Without seamless integration of these two services, Kindle books and Audible.com, it becomes a big frustration very quickly. Did I mention that Audible.com charges $14.95 PER MONTH for membership? Not user friendly in a recession/depression environment! How about a "no strings attached" membership? Finally, Audible.com only permits 3 Kindle devices to be on your account. For my household, with 6 Kindles, this doesn't beget customer satisfaction, or a desire to become a member of Audible.com.Additionally, some of the free books linked to Whispersync for Voice I had previously purchased. Unfortunately, those editions would not link to Whispersync for Voice, meaning I had to re-purchase (albeit free) the book (different edition) to link to and then purchase (again with a free promotion) the audio book from Audible.com. For a paid version of a Kindle book that also has an audible version available but no link to Whispersync (those links are listed on the book product page) means you have to use a particular Kindle book with the particular companion Audible.com audible book. Bummer.7. Ads. Ads. Ads. For $199 I expect an Ad-free environment. Not here! You have to "opt-out" for an additional charge ($15). BAD MOVE for Amazon. Even then, once you opt-out, the continual "suggestions" are annoying and intrusive to the extreme. This does not exist on the original Kindle Fire.8. No SD card slot, a continuing Amazon deficiency (especially when dealing with content when you are out of Wi-Fi range), and no user replaceable battery. This is where my Kindle 1 shines. I keep categories of books on different SD cards because (obviously) the drive in K1 is inadequate to the task of taking my entire library along. The Kindle Keyboard (4 GB storage) houses my complete library, but not the Kindle Touch (2GB storage). You may ask, why is this important with the cloud drive available? Because ever since Amazon ripped my paid-for copy of George Orwell's 1984 off my Kindle without my permission, I do not trust my purchased content exclusively to Amazon's cloud drive. I back it up immediately to the computer.9. No Favorites section below the Carousel without going through the "Favorites" Star icon. Great when you can find it, annoying when you can't.10. Inconsistent displays on the Carousel. Not all items are displayed, they mysteriously disappear and reappear. When you tap them to open sometimes they do, and other times they just shake in place without opening. Other times, when trying to remove them from the Carousel, once you "tap and hold", the concurrent menu allowing you to remove the item from the device, the carousel or add/remove from Favorites does not appear at all. The "shimmy" effect of a vibrating icon on the Carousel is very disturbing (at least to me), making me wonder if it's trying to crash (aka a computer crash).12. No YouTube. No YouTube app that works.13. Email display is horrific both in portrait and landscape modes. Once an email is opened you have to scroll to read side-to-side, with a column list of your emails on the left (in landscape mode) which cannot be changed.14. Android Apps for Kindle Fire purchased for the original Kindle Fire may or may not (mostly not) work on the new Kindle Fire HD. When I asked about this, Customer Service told me they were "working on it." Right out of the box this is inexcusable. It's like saying, "You can't have all your Kindle books which you purchased on this device because it is not going to work yet for those items".15. Huge screen glare problem. Just gotta love seeing my face and the room around me while doing anything with this Kindle! The "anti-glare screen protector" recommended by Amazon is anything but anti-glare, and (conveniently) no other anti-glare screen protectors offered will fit the KFHD.16. The "recommended" case by Amazon only allows the KF to be installed one way and the display to face one way when using the stand, so you can't watch a movie even if you flip it over to view a movie in landscape mode while charging. Unfortunately, due to the location of the power cable (when plugged in), this makes it impossible to watch a movie using the case as a stand while the power cord is plugged in. The stand use of the case is unstable. If you read in bed, as I do, I find this to be a massive problem. The RooCase for the Original Kindle Fire accomplished both tasks for the original KF nicely.17. Camera only works with Skype (and Facebook with a lot of fiddling with an app to make it happen).My advice is PASS ON THIS PURCHASE. WAIT FOR KINDLE FIRE HD 3. Mine is going back, and I would advise anyone wanting a Kindle Fire to buy a refurbished original KF from Amazon (if any) or go to eBay. This one is too expensive and too buggy--perhaps released too quickly before fixing engineering and software glitches. For me, the Cons far outweighed the Pros to the point that this device is not for me. Hopefully my observations will help someone in their purchase decision. I really did want to keep this device; however, given the financial times and the inherent problems I have experienced with the KFHD, it is not worth the effort if you already have a Kindle Fire Original.Finally, given the above, I could not also justify buying an 8.9" screen for the larger KFHD either. Buy an iPad instead if you want a bigger screen and easy email handling (yes, I have and use an iPad).For the convenience, I hope one day Amazon adds Text to Speech to the original KF, but til then my Kindle Keyboard keeps on keepin' on. Fine for me. The newer editions are (for me) a waste of time and money.REVIEW UPDATE:Even though I sent mine back, I decided to try one more time because I got a new one as gift. Because of continuing hardware problems, I am now on my 5th return of this item to Amazon (LOVE their customer service) by their request. KFHD #6 still has issues which cannot be resolved.NOTE WELL: MY REVIEW IS A COMPARISON OF THE NEW KFHD TO THE 1ST GEN KINDLE FIRE ONLY. Several comments to my review have been rude and mean, which has kept me from updating this review until now (Jan 2013).My 6th KFHD has solved the video color problem very well, but the previous 1,2,3,4,5 ones had speakers blow out when connected to a bluetooth device (ipod classic and an ipod touch). Bummer. I have not connected this one to a bluetooth speaker (Bose), nor will I in the future.STILL have email problems. Started using the paid email app which approximates the display of the amazon email app on the original KF. However, my ISP uses a Barracuda Spam Firewall Filter that sends an email for me to connect to my quarantined inbox to check if any emails need to go to the inbox rather than the quarantine box. The Barracuda link goes to a web page, but the web page only loads half-way and will NOT allow me to access the quarantine inbox. The old KF had no problem with this. None. The new one does not allow this function. AMAZON CUSTOMER SERVICE HAS ADMITTED THAT THIS IS A BROWSER GLITCH ON THEIR PART AND THEY HAVE NO INTENTION OF FIXING IT. 3 customer service agents have told me it is a known issue that Amazon will NOT solve. End of discussion. So if your ISP uses Barracuda, BEWARE.AS COMPARED TO THE ORIGINAL FIRE, THIS ONE IS STILL A DISAPPOINTMENT for me. As for you, only you can decide.
summary: Keep your old Kindle Fire, this is a dud! Too many bugs!!

reviewText: This is a rewrite of my original review, the one that garnered all the helpful votes you see, now that this particular Kindle has been replaced with a new and improved replacement, it's time for retrospective reviews for a device few should buy given better valued alternatives.My original review warned that Amazon had a history of not providing updated operating systems to their legacy devices. And that has again proven true. The current Fire HD, the one released in 2013, is running a new operating system called Fire OS 3.0, which is based upon Android 4.2.2 (this is according to Wikipedia) whereas this device is stuck on a fork of Android 4.0.3); I've called Kindle support and the nice lady tells me that this is the situation and she has no information about it changing. By comparison, I purchased an iPad Mini a few months after my Kindle Fire HD, and it has since been upgraded to iOS 7 and Apple has scheduled it for an iOS 8 upgrade in the fall. This is not a device with a software future.So, I've had both this device and an iPad Mini in my house for well over a year, and my children and I have both hugely favored the Mini in terms of every use case except the easy consumption of books. The Mini has a nicer, smoother browser which combined with its larger screen make it a far superior web experience, an easier to navigate operating system: the standard carousel view of the Kindle gets old very fast as you want to navigate to another app. And iOS has the best selection of optimized tablet apps of any mobile device. The Kindle has proven a nice way for my son to spontaneously find something to read; as long as I can stomach the occasional $6 charge for a cheap book. And it's been convenient sometimes to drop the kids into the Freetime mode of curated all-you-can-eat children's content. But in general, we get more use out of the Mini; to the point I lost the Kindle somewhere in the house for a couple months and nobody complained or even asked where it might be (it was under a stack of books).The hardware has been solid if not a technological feast. Whereas I've twice had to go and get my iPad Mini replaced via AppleCare due to a drop, the Fire HD is completely unscathed and looks as new as the day it came out of the box. Most of this is use, but still, it's solidly built. However, I'm constantly reminded by the huge difference in screen size between a widescreen 7 inch tablet like this device and a 4:3 nearly 8 inch tablet like the Mini; there's just so much more content visible on the Mini and common activities like web browsing seem so less confined. The Kindle does have a lovely high resolution screen and text looks great on it. Speedwise, the Kindle chugs along; it's not ridiculously underpowered like the original Kindle Fire, but you wouldn't call it snappy. My original review said the design of the device was something "...future Kindles can build upon and refine..." well that turned out to be wrong, not that the new design is bad.Connectivity has been fine. I've never had any problems with WiFi, and the times I've needed to use Bluetooth--for playing music to speakers for instance--have worked flawlessly, better than iOS 6 at being reliable. I wish that the charging port didn't look so much like the adjacent mini-HDMI port as finding which to plug into is a pain. The worst thing about the construction are the buttons which are hard to locate, and cheap feeling. The microphone/headphone jack has been a bit unreliable when it comes to using headphone controls, sometimes a click is missed.The ecosystem has been mediocre. I don't have much experience with Google's Play Store, but certainly as an iOS user I have a better App store and a wider collection of accessories, peripherals and built in services. For instance, I'd never lose my iPad in my house as long as it had charge enough for me to make it beep with the Find My Phone app. Many people have commented in this review that I should point out the alternative of buying a Nexus 7 from Google, and while I can't recommend what I haven't used, it seems likely shoppers should give that a glance.Anyway, I'm glad to have provided a critical review which has helped so many shoppers. I'd say that no one should buy this product as it is now priced--I'm sure Amazon expects you might want one of their newer offering--and I wish you luck with your buying decision.

reviewText: I got this specifically because I have a lot of Amazon music and video content I purchased, so staying in that ecosystem makes sense. I use it on the train, download movies and tv shows to it to watch during the commute. I also download my music from the cloud and listen to it. Synced right up with my bluetooth headphones.Screen is very sharp and the ICS OS is fine, since I rarely venture out of the Amazon media players. I bought the 32 GB just to limit the frequency I'd have to download additional content to watch/play on the device, but probably could have lived with the 16Gb. But for the extra $50, and without an expansion slot, I figured it was worth it to double the storage. Keep in mind there are always system resources that take up space, so your actual storage space is never the reported max, so that also convinced me to go with the larger capacity.Sound is okay from the speakers, but you want to use headphones or an external speaker. I haven't connected the Kindle via the HDMI port yet, but nice that it has it. Although, we already have devices that play Amazon video content (PS3 and TV, plus BD players), so probably won't ever end up doing that.Size is perfect for what I wanted. I wanted something larger than a smartphone, but not as large as my laptop. I hold it in my hand or on my lap during the commute, so too wide would be annoying and tiresome, but too small is hard to see with lights, glare, etc. This is the ideal size for my use. It's not too thick and is light enough. It has more heft than i was expecting, but it's not heavy by any means.I considered other Android based tablets but it was the amount of Amazon content I already owned that swayed me. I have limited Google Play content as well, which I understand you can root the device to install the player. I may do that to be able to access that content as well, but it will void the warranty, so may hold off on that until later date.I think if this was going to be more of a fully functional device for me (i.e., check email, surf the web, use more android apps, etc.), I'd want a larger display. However, considering how I was going to use (on the commute) and where (on the train), this was good enough. I have a laptop I use for mobile computing (e.g., email, productivity, web browsing), and a desktop that I use for gaming, movies, etc., so this is strictly for entertainment outside the home. And for that purpose, the pricepoint and size are perfect.

reviewText: Ok, I am normally a pretty big fan of Amazon devices. The Kindle has been groundbreaking for reading and media consumption. The Kindle Fire HD was a big disappointment for everyone in our family though.I bought this as a birthday gift for a 13 year old. She had an original Kindle and loved it for reading. She wanted an iPad, but I bought this instead. She has a lot of friends with Android tablets and thought it would be cool to have a non iOS device.First the pros:Build and screen are quite nice. The device is a little heavy, but feels sturdy in the hand. The bevel looks like something for a kid, but I figure that was part of the design.App Store killed the deal for us:The biggest complaint is that this is not really an Android tablet. Apps her friends have on their Android tablets are not available. The crippled store makes it so things like Instagram are not available. Now one app she could have lived with by having it on her phone. But we have found dozens of apps that are missing from this app store, but are available to Android. Without the apps that kids want it is really hard for her to be happy using the device.I spoke to people I work with who have Kindle Fires and all of them told me they had another device for games because the app store just doesn't get the games they wanted to play. Then what is the point of keeping this? If I am going to want a second device anyway, might as well get rid of this one.It wasn't just my daughter wanting another device either. I also tried to use the Kindle for the past week while we have been deciding what to do about it. The interface is just weird to me. The little swiping left right to find stuff feels like I am staring at some jukebox from 1950. It is not fluid and doesn't let me organize anything the way I want it. You are sort of stuck in iPod 1990 scroll land with no way to customize it.Summary:The device itself is ok. But it is some sort of no mans lands between devices. If you are going to make a custom app store and break the ecosystem then don't call it an android tablet. It is misleading. I expected that from Nook, but not from Amazon.So this device will be going on eBay, the first time I have done such with an Amazon product.

reviewText: The 7" Kindle Fire was the perfect gift for both of my kids. The size is just right for them, light weight and they can take it with them anywhere. All the games work great and the graphics are fabulous. Very happy with the purchase so far.

First let me say that if your MAIN focus is to read books and magazines, listen to music, and/or play games, this is a very nice little device.However I can't tell you how disappointed I am with the WEB interface on this thing!It's basically KLUNKY and USER-UNFRIENDLY re the web.The main thing is that it does not act like a web browser. Why re-invent the wheel so that if you are accustomed to using a web browser you now have to learn a whole new way of doing things? It's dumb and frustrating.I am a web expert. I use the web to make money and I spent at least 8 hours every day on the web. So I know how to navigate the web and how to do just about anything on a computer.I understand that the FireHD is NOT a computer and I knew it would be limited in some things. However I would think that accessing the web would be one of those things that it should and would do well. But it's NOT.Let me give you a couple examples:I wanted to set up my email so I could get some kind of visual notification when I get an email. I don't want just a sound notification because when I use this I do not require sound so do not want to turn my sound up (as it would bother people around me) nor do I want to wear earplugs or a headset all the time as I really don't need to hear sounds other than for notifications. So what I would expect is that there be something like a Windows "system tray" which I could set up to notify me that I received mail, or something like an Android phone notification. (Hey how about a VIBRATOR on it, Amazon? That would work, too!)Another day I wanted to check the local bus schedules. I got to the web site, clicked on the bus schedule I wanted to look at and it was a pdf. My Kindle Fire appeared to be downloading the pdf but a) it did not OPEN nor give me the option to open the pdf; and b) I could not find it downloaded anywhere on my KindleFireHD. So basically I had to get to a computer to do the exact same process, except that with my computer it easily and automatically opened the pdf allowing me to get the info I needed!I don't want to make this review too long but basically the point is that this thing is just plain LOUSY for using the internet! So many times I run into problems with it not accessing the info I need to access.My advice to Amazon is that they make it act more like a computer web browser like Firefox or Chrome or even the dreaded IE would be better than what they have!I gave this to my wife because she mostly uses it for games, with limited internet use (however, even she finds it very klunky to use the internet and often she also has to use the computer to access the info she wants because somehow it's too hard to get to it via the FireHD).I would never recommend this to anyone because the internet usage is such a major part of our lives now, and I would recommend someone spend a little more and get a Tablet that has the ability to use a browser such as Firefox or Chrome.While this works for games and books, so will any tablet and yet the tablet is going to give you a much better internet experience.I am surprised this thing has so many good reviews. As far as I'm concerned it's a monumental FAIL and I wish I'd have returned it.p.s. Go to the Kindle Support page here on Amazon and have a look around at some of the questions that are not being answered, and the problems people are having with basic functions like Notifications of email, opening attachments, etc.
summary: Don't buy this if you want to use the web on it

reviewText: The default software on the Kindle Fire HD is intrusive, restrictive, and lacking in the ways that mattered to me. Every application, book, etc. that you've opened is kept in order (you have some freedom to choose what displays first, though) of access. I did not like this at all nor did my wife, the reader.Google Play cannot be loaded onto the device without rooting, even though the device is Android at its core. Rooting runs the risk of bricking the device and probably voids the warranty.Bottom line: If you are purchasing this device as a tablet, you may be disappointed. If you are okay with being restricted to the Amazon App Store, don't mind not having freedom over the launcher used (unless rooted...but even then custom backgrounds aren't possible on the currently shipped software version), and aren't interested in modifying anything about the device, this review does not pertain to you. If I was in that category, this would have been a 5/5 star review.After modification of the device, this is actually a 5/5 star review...but it isn't an Amazon Kindle anymore, so I cannot give it that rating. I love my tablet now but I did not love it out of the box.

1st, I have the Kindle Fire HD 7" with 32 GB of storage and ads enabled.If you are a book junkie, news junkie, or movie buff like me, then you will love the Kindle. You can carry around in your hand a whole library of large or small books and read them at your leisure, which can be just about anywhere. I think that aspect of it is great.There are also all kinds of games for it. I like a handful of the basic time-wasters, but otherwise I stay away from them.It does not have the basic card reader. It is designed with the idea that all of your storage will be on Amazon's Cloud Storage. Amazon gives you unlimited storage for the materials which you purchase from them, plus 5 GB for personal data. You can't transfer images from your favorite camera onto it, unless it has built-in WiFi (maybe). The Kindle is designed to rely only on it's built-in camera. I don't consider the built-in camera to be real great. Plus I consider the built-in camera awkward to use. It seems like the main idea of it is to take pictures of the user. Use with video calls and video conferencing would be ideal for it.Unlike the Netbooks, which were popular a couple of years ago, this tablet does not replace a computer in any sense of the word. You will still need a computer in addition to this tablet.Also, while I am on computer issues, Amazon's instructions say that this table will connect to any computer. This idea does not seem to be true with some computers and operating systems. My computer would be an example. The Kindle transfer system relies on the newest version of the Windows Media Player. I am running Windows 7-64 Premium on a 1 year old Toshiba. It has an AMD 64 bit processor and the 64 bit version of Windows 7. (Amazon and Microsoft both indicate that I am a minority with this choice.) I have the Windows Media Player on my computer. However, Microsoft gives me the message that the newest version of their Media Player will NOT run on my system. Apparently, my version of Windows Media Player is upgraded as far as Microsoft is going to upgrade it. (I never use it anyway.) It also appears that Kindle can not transfer files to my computer without the newest version. To get files from one computer to the other, it seems that I will have to email them to myself. (This is going to be a pain.)WiFi connections are problematic. That said, the Kindle version seems to be more problematic then most. I travel all over the USA. If you are in an area where there is a lot of WiFi routers, then the Kindle seems to get confused and refuses to work. Or you start running into security issues with everyone.I mentioned before that I am a movie buff. There is not room on it's internal storage to download a bunch of movies to it, and there is no external storage except on Amazon. I have even tried attaching an adapter and card reader card to it. This idea didn't work. Kindle won't recognize the card.I purchased a Bluetooth keyboard which works fine with it. But while I can pair up my computer to the Kindle with a Bluetooth connection, I still can not transfer files to/from my computer to the Kindle using it. (Don't know why, yet.)One thing that I have noticed is that this is a great idea to increase Amazon's business. I have purchased several apps and books from Amazon for it. Books are usually a lot cheaper to buy for use on Kindle. Apps are usually very cheap. And it is really nice to have a whole library to read at any given point where I have extra time. The built-in reader which reads books back to you is another great feature. I like have it read to me while I sit back and relax. (I am reminded of teachers asking me in high school if I was reading with my eyes closed and my head laying on the books.)Another issue that I have run into is the Kindle headphone-speaker plug. I am working trying to find out what works and what doesn't work with it. I have one set of headphones which will work with it, and they sound great. But most headphones and speakers won't work with it. The receiver socket of the plug-in area is recessed, and only a plug with an indented collar will make a connection. Standard speakers and headphones for other devices don't seem to work with it since their connecting plugs don't slide inside the socket far enough.The sound from the Kindle is great. The video is great. It is easy to read. There is a ton of things that you could do with it.In short, the Kindle is a great idea. But it still needs work.Update: Sept 18, 2013I have ordered many things from Amazon using my Kindle Fire HD.But it hit me that not all of the items available from Amazon will show up on the Kindle when browsing and placing orders. An example would be a jacket that I just received. I am a big person, and need big clothes. I ordered the largest size of a jacket that I liked using my Kindle Fire HD. It barely fits me. I looked at the jacket that I ordered on my home computer and saw that Amazon offers the jacket the next 2 sizes larger, and in additional colors. The additional larger sizes and colors where not showing on my Kindle when I placed the order.As I said before, the Kindle fine for reading books, magazines, and for a person's personal entertainment. In fact, it is great for that. But it does not replace a computer.
summary: Great for Amazon fans. Does not replace a computer.

Hello reader. I'm a time traveler from the short future. I've traveled back in time to answer questions you have already asked me about the Kindle Fire HD. I do this so that you know exactly what to expect. There is no Temporal Prime Directive stopping me.*** ADS: Are they really that big a deal? ***Answer: It depends. You see, some people misunderstand an "ad" from "related info". They think that anything showing on your screen that you didn't explicitly ask for must be an "ad". This is faulty. The Kindle Fire HD does have ads on its lock screen. That is the ONLY place you see ads. They are not in the books, not in the X-Ray, not in the book info, not in your Library. Yes, the ads are full screen, but again, lock screen only. Also, the ads rotate; there are roughly 6-7 of them and they cycle. You won't care about most of them. I found some funny; like an ad for a Titanic Blu-ray, it's like Amazon momentarily forgot that it's supposed to pitch me on the Instant Video. But then there are some really good ones, like the first ad I got presented was a no-strings $5 credit for the Instant Video section, which is absolutely awesome. There's one for the Kindle Fire HD's case, which I had already bought. They're simply not intrusive.In your Library, you will be presented with recommendations similar to the Amazon website. These are NOT ads. They're recommendations. They're there to help you if you're looking for new things to read. No, you can't disable that service, but you can readily ignore it. It doesn't harm you, it doesn't sell you anything if you don't choose it. But it's there so you at least HAVE the choice to find new books. IF you're a hermit who doesn't want to be told nuthin, the Kindle Fire HD is not for you. IN fact, none of the Kindles are, because even the Kindle Keyboard has recommendations when you go to the Kindle Book store. This is nothing new; they just present them directly into the device as part of its tighter integration.Now one thing I will say: put the Parental Controls on if you plan on handing this to a kid (though I suggest you do not. If you want to give your kid a tablet for some bizarre reason get them a Nexus 7 instead.) The reason I say this: It's terribly easy to purchase stuff from the ads. It asked me for a login the first time but beyond that, nothing. So yes, I can see how kids might end up purchasing stuff they're not supposed to.In short: if you're holding back because the ads bother you, they're NOT intrusive. If they bother you that much you really need to find a hobby. You know what it feels like? You know those posters (Or sometimes digital signage) at the airport with a backlight behind them that you sort of have no choice but to see? That's what they feel like. But you block them out, and every now and then, you see one that catches your eye and you might look for more info.*** SCREEN: Is it really that good? ***Answer: It depends. I have the original Fire and I can safely say it's leaps and bounds superior to the original. But I also have a Nexus 7 and it's a close comparison. The screen quality is there, the viewing angle is there. I found their announcement about glare to be mostly hype; while it is less glossy and reflective than the Nexus or the original Fire, the difference is minimal enough that a regular user might not even be able to tell. The only screen protectors were glossy, which I found to be a glaring (no pun intended) oversight on Amazon's part. I didn't expect them to go all matte, but I expected them to do more, I guess.That said, the screen is reasonably responsive. I am not a fan of Amazon's keyboard and you can't do anything about it; most of the good keyboard alternatives on the Amazon Appstore are blocked from the Fire HD. You could sideload but it's a bit of a pain to switch keyboards.In terms of brightness, contrast, colors, etc. I have no complaints whatsoever. Things do pop out at you and text is a lot more crisp than before. The black levels are also fairly impressive, as well. Don't let the Amazon software fool you into thinking it's supposed to be black; it's not. That's their color scheme and it will trick you. But if you pull up something like the cover to Bram Stoker's "Dracula" which is pitch black you will see what I mean.*** AUDIO: Is the audio improved like they say? ***Answer: it depends. You see, if you're asking whether the sound is better than the original Fire, that's an absolute resounding YES, no question. However, if you're asking whether the audio is going to blow you away...probably not. For you see, the audio on this device, while it is louder, isn't necessarily "better". It's amplified with no real bass to it. For audiobooks it's not an issue, but if you plan to listen to music, be prepared to be disappointed especially if you're streaming it from Amazon MP3 and it's been converted to 256kbps. Can you say tinny?*** All you're doing is bashing it! ***I realize that's what it seems like, but honestly, I'm getting those out of the way. Frankly, I like the FIre. I was considering getting the 8.9" 4G version, but my experience with the Nexus 7 has told me that I really do like the form factor of the 7". Additionally, I'm not sure I can justify the $100 - $300 premium for the larger screen, and I have unlimited 4G hotspot I already pay for. It just didn't make sense. For you it might, though.Great things about the Fire HD:- Battery. I streamed SKY.FM (don't ask how I got it done, but I did) all day at work today and listened to audiobooks, AND sat with the screen on just now while typing this, and I'm just now at 58%. That's from a full charge, so you figure just under 16 hours. Not bad.- Performance. I have had a few hiccups, and it crashed when I was first setting it up, AND Amazon's own browser claimed to be incompatible with the Amazon store at first, but after all that, it was great.- Integration. The one thing that was weird about the original Fire was that you were jarred out of the experience if you went to any of the stores. On the newer Fire HD, everything is seamless, even the Audible store. You never feel like you're taken out of the process except when replying to ad offers. That seamless transition is something even Apple hasn't perfected, but it works well here.- Offers. Amazon throws stuff at you just for trying things out. Try Audible, get a free audiobook AND a free credit (with which you can get another audiobook). Try Prime, get a month free (I was already Prime so I didn't get this). Try an ad, get a $5 video credit. Buy something, get some credit towards Amazon MP3. It's a pleasant experience, and it makes me want to spend there knowing that I'll eventually be offered something.I can tell you this though. DO NOT buy this expecting a standard tablet experience. You will not be satisfied. Amazon has gone out of their way to isolate the Fire to its own ecosystem. You can root it and experiment, but I find that a waste of time. IF all you want is a tablet, get the Nexus 7. Get the Fire if you want an Amazon experience in a tablet form factor; because it will do that for you.
summary: A step in the proper direction. But just shy.

I'll start with a list of pros and cons for some who may not want to read a lengthy review.PROS:*cost*size*speed*brightness adjustment (both for reading in-program and for OS); I will also mention Kindle's alternative color reading options here as their sepia mode is very easy on the eyesCONS:*messy OS; carousel*lack of hard home button*slim profile volume/power button*2 portsI decided to give the Kindle Fire HD a try for three reasons: size, price point, and because I already use the Kindle app on other devices. I've found the physical experience with the tablet to be quite enjoyable: I can use it one handed; It is not overtly heavy; and (perhaps most importantly) it's compact size makes it more portable than other devices I have used. It fits in my purse very easily. One of my major pros as a reader is when the brightness can be adjusted. Kindle's app is great for e-reading since it is a reader. It also helps if you're watching movies late at night and don't want to wake a spouse.On to the cons. It seems I have a lot of them, don't I? First off I'll conquer the elephant in the room...it's riding a carousel. Kindle's carousel is ridiculous. I have tried cleaning items off of it, adding items to favorites, even investigating alternative launchers (which don't appear to be available for this device yet, without rooting it, which I'm not willing to do at the moment).... I think it looks disastrous. What would be so wrong with a plain home screen with little icons of your apps and books? I don't need all 15 of my recently synced PDFs to pop up there indefinitely, or until I go and mark them as read and then remove them again. The favorites option doesn't seem to work - I'm trying to bookmark a few like Pandora, Facebook and the like and I'm disappointed. Amazon really could stand to improve this feature.Here is another beef I have. I paid $15 so I wouldn't have lock screen ads, but I'm stuck with random, boring, un-customizable lock screen images? I call bullshit. I love photography and some of the images are pretty, don't get me wrong, but I want to know I'm picking up MY kindle, not Suzie Sweet Briar's. That's going to happen if there's a lovely picture I put on that lock screen staring back at me. (Yes, this is if I don't happen to have a case on it. I ordered one, it didn't fit. Different review.) The OS is the leader of your user experience. It doesn't matter if I like your e-reader app. If every time I pick up my kindle I cringe at what I'm looking at, I'm not going to use my device. Sigh.In so far as the physical cons, which comprise the rest of my complaints, they consist of the following: there is no hard home button. I dislike 100% touch screen items but because of the PROS I listed before I was willing to overlook this. I like having the feature where I can double tap to hit my home page. It will take some re-training to remember to look for the little home icon. It's annoying. The slim profile volume buttons are also irritating - you either have to look or guess which ones you are hitting because they are in line with the device. Some could say this is a pro; I consider it a nuisance to either a)always use the menus or b)look at the side to figure out which is which. Either way I'm interrupting my reading/viewing/listening experience to do something with the volume. Final con...what the heck do we need 2 ports for? 1 for syncing and charging is sufficient. It's also on the long side of the device, which is odd, and makes for odd looking cases in some situations.As of right now, I'm going to give it another week or two and see if it grows on me, or see if I can get an alternative launcher to load...but even for the size and price point, I am really hoping all of these Apple Mini reviews are true. Best of luck in your shopping!

Let me begin this by saying that I used to be an "early adopter". I had to have it when it first came out. I've stopped doing that, but in this case I wish I had bought the first Fire. From using a friend's I was excited when they finally announced the second gen devices. The original was simple to use and did most things I wanted it to. This one is incredibly hard to figure out, even with years of techy experience and is more limited in its use.PROS -Feels solid and well built.Anti-glare screen is nice, and the screen is vibrant. It's not Retina, but then it didn't cost like one so I'm OK with that.Some have reported it being slow and unresponsive, but I haven't had much of a problem except when in apps I know have problems from them doing the same to my phone. Videos streamed from Amazon look really good.Book reading is surprisingly good for a backlit screen. Page turns are quick and although they lack the book like "charm" of the Kindle reader page turns it is an acceptable substitute.Screen brightness is good and you can see the screen pretty well outdoors. I have turned off automatic screen brightness though. I find the values it chooses too bright in most cases and have mine set slightly less than 50%.CONS -No AC adapter included. Would that have really been that much of a stretch to include?No flash support. UPDATE: Well...no official flash support. Thanks to the comment from TomT below I was able to install both flash and my preferred browser (Dolphin) in a few minutes. Google Flash 11.1 apk and follow the xda developer links...will walk you right through it. Now if I can get Google Voice working so I can use sonar I'll be a happy camper. Have added a star since it was this easy. That still doesn't negate the fact that it should have been included in the first place with so many sites still using Flash.The charge and HDMI ports are on the long edge rather than the short as is on my other Kindles (and the original Fire I believe). When you want to do HDMI out to a TV you can only turn it one way if you want to tilt it up which may, depending on the case you buy, totally defeat the stand in the case. In the case of the Marware leather rotating case you can't close the case when charging because the ports are to the inside.Volume and On-Off buttons are flush with the case and almost impossible to find by feel. Since the only visual cue for which way you are holding it is the camera lens this makes it difficult in a darkened room.No GPS. This isn't a deal breaker, but would have been nice. I suppose they thought since it needs wireless people wouldn't use it like that, but I could always turn on my phone's Mobile Hotspot to use Google maps IF I had a GPS.The ads. I own other Kindles and have never felt the need to turn them off. They were unobtrusive and didn't really affect my use of the device. I even went for them occasionally. The ones on the new Kindle are ridiculous. Everywhere you turn they are in your face just waiting for an errant touch to purchase something you don't mean to and taking up screen space. People who care for children or the elderly should be extra vigilant for unintended purchases.Lack of many apps in the app store that I use daily on my Android phone and would use on the Kindle if they were there. It's clear Amazon doesn't want to take any chances that you might stream something online that doesn't belong to them. No TNT app, no USA app, no CW app. I assume the others that I don't use like HBO and Showtime aren't there either? No support for PowerDVD Remote and PowerDVD Mobile which would allow me to stream my own personal videos from my network rather than having to either upload them to the cloud or onto the device. Can't access my Dropbox either. I use my phone as a remote constantly when streaming from my HTPC to my TV and I was hoping I could use the Kindle that way too.Apps that work perfectly well on my phone throw error after error on the Kindle's "special" version. Examples: Words with Friends, no paid version and ads lock up the device. Tweetcaster constantly throws the 350 connections per hour message and I am not a heavy user. It throws this one when all I do is check it once in a while and have it set on manual refresh. I ended up in Twitter Jail the first night I had the Kindle and I didn't tweet a single thing! Never had this happen on my phone.Every app you download results in a "purchase" email from Amazon...even the free ones. I have an avalanche of them in my inbox just from setting it up. (Yes, I know this happens for phones as well. I make the comment to point it out to those that don't know. Amazon should have a better way worked out to handle this by now and since Kindle is part of their proprietary environment and since Kindle is a part of that this is part of owning one.)The Carousel? I hate it. Everything goes on it as soon as you load or use it even if you don't want it to. There may be a way to fine tune this, but if there is I haven't found it yet. I put a few favorite songs on the device for when I'm not near wireless and it showed each individual song on the Carousel. The UI is cluttered and as far as I can see there is no way to alter it to better serve your personal needs. No way to clear the Carousel either. You have to remove items one by one. (If anyone knows how to change this please do let me know.)The main screen is obviously front loaded to get you to buy stuff..with the few things things that get around the spoon feeding of ads and buying stuff all the way to the right like photos and web.UPDATE: I had not attempted to use the camera. There is no software included to make use of the camera. The User guide says you can download Skype and that it MAY work with other apps in the store, but there is no way to use it without downloading something and experimentation to see what apps might work with it. Why include the camera if they aren't going to give you something to help use it?No alarm clock app included. Now I know there are apps that will do this, but it's pretty much a basic inclusion on most mobile devices these days.Haven't decided if I will return or wait and hope Amazon offers some software updates that make it more acceptable. It's a brilliant hardware upgrade hogtied by Amazon's watered-down version of Android and the lack of basic apps like camera/alarm that we have all come to expect. I haven't tested the HDMI out yet, since my micro-HDMI cable hasn't arrived yet. Will update this review next week when I get that.
summary: First Fire...not sure I want to keep it

reviewText: I currently own the 2nd generation iPad and the Kindle keyboard device.Reasons for purchasing the Kindle Fire HD:Kindle Keyboard (KK): I liked the ability to change my font size and the ability to read in bright sunshine with their e-ink technology. I also liked the smallness and lightweight of my KK that I could throw it in my purse and took it everywhere I go. While I liked my Kindle keyboard, it could be cumbersome to manipulate using the device's buttons. I was spoiled with using my iPad.iPad: The glare from iPad made it difficult to read my books and magazines. Also, I couldn't change the fonts within the Kindle app for the iPad at least the books I had downloaded.Though I enjoy using my iPad, it can be a bit heavy to carry around as well as hold in my hand for long periods of time (e.g. reading books). It was time to find another device.It made a lot of sense for me to look into the Kindle Fire HD as next device/gadget. I already have hundreds of Kindle books and I'm also an Amazon Prime member.Research:I read the specs and user reviews here on Amazon. I also saw the comparisons between the Kindle Fire HD and the iPad. I was pretty much sold on this device, but I had to see and feel the device in my hand. There's nothing like having that touchy-feeling experience before making the purchase.I went to my local Staples store to test out the 7" Kindle Fire HD (KFHD). Automatically, there were three things that caught my attention: the screen, ease of use, and the dual speakers. The screen is beautiful! I could see and read the text/books even with the slight glare from the store's lights. It wasn't annoying at all. The next thing I immediately noticed was how easy it was to maneuver around and use the KFHD. It was second nature for me to swipe and pinch and expand the screen. Just like using the iPad. Lastly, I listened to some sample music was blown away with the quality of the dual speakers. I had the volume turned down and noticed how crisp and clear the sound was.I also played around with the 8.9" version of this device. Once I had it in my hand, it reminded me of my iPad: the weight and size. I played around with this device and noticed that having a bigger screen was nice, but that is why I have my iPad.I was thankful I was able to hold both devices in my hand and be able to make a sound decision.So, here I am with my new 7" Kindle Fire HD.Likes:-The bright clear screen for reading and watching movies-Ease of use. Flick down the top bar to access the KFHD settings.-Easy to connect to my home router/WiFi-Ability to use my existing iPad charging block/adapter-Use of Amazon Cloud to retrieve my books and picturesDislikes:-When I look up apps to purchase, it appears somewhat slow to see the information and icons-Battery life. I'm spoiled by the long battery life of my iPad as well as from my Kindle keyboard. I'm looking into tweaking my KFHD to see if I can disable some settings.Summary:I bought the 7" Kindle Fire HD with 16GB of storage and with the ads. I had some points and a gift card to use which brought the price down quite a bit.I'm glad I got the 7" version as it complements my existing iPad. The intent was not to replace my iPad as that is my primary tablet device.This 7" KFHD has found a place in my purse right next to my iPhone. I will use the KFHD as an everyday portable device (reading books, checking email, and web browsing) while I'm on the go.I'm really happy with my new gadget. I can't find any real faults with this device. I'm enjoying my KFHD experience.I'll be back with updates including what kind of battery life I will be getting, apps downloaded and used, and any tips and tricks I come across. Stay tuned!

I was blown away by the sound quality. Absolutely stunning sound on this device. Video is great, but it's the quality of the sound that really sells it. You get quite a lot for the cheap price. Absolutely worth the $199.

This is my 3rd new Kindle Fire HD in 8 months. The first one I had, the left speaker went out. I guess this is a somewhat common problem. Customer service was EXCELLENT!!! They quickly replaced it with a new one. The second one I couldn't even get through the registration process because the screen would either freeze up on me, or these weird lines (which looked like a bar code at times) would gradually appear on the screen and cover 80% of it. Again, customer service was EXCELLENT!!! They quickly replaced it with a new one. The third one has MANY problems. It would suddenly start downloading apps that were already downloaded. Sometimes this would happen while I was using the same app, causing it to close down. Sometimes 2 apps would mysteriously start downloading. Videos would say they were loading, but then it would just sit there and never play. Downloaded apps would suddenly disappear and I would have to download them again. Videos would start playing, then stop and my carousel would appear. The screen would freeze up. Just too many problems. When I called customer service, we went through all the trouble shooting as usual with no success including deregistering and reregistering. To their credit, they offered to send out a 4th new one, but at this point, I don't have ANY faith in this product. I would say I use the Kindle less than an hour a day. They've never been dropped, spilled on, sat in direct sunlight, or anything else that would have caused these things to happen. I know other people have Kindles that work great, but mine did not. I'm returning this Kindle Fire HD for a refund and not looking back. Time to invest in a more reliable tablet. Sorry Kindle and Amazon, but thanks for the GREAT customer service.9/27/2013 UPDATE - Well it seems like the usual confusion with big companies. If you've read up above, you know about all the problems I had. When I contacted Kindle customer service, they ultimately offered me an 80% refund. When I called back to accept (after giving it some thought), I was told by a different agent that Amazon will not accept returns or offer ANY kind of refund on the Kindle Fire HD after the initial 30 days of the ORIGINAL purchase. As you can imagine, I was not happy to hear this, so my only option was to have them ship me a 4th Kindle Fire HD. After hanging up the phone, I was checking my e-mail and was surprised to get an e-mail from Amazon asking me "Did I solve your problem?" I clicked on the "NO" link and was asked to provide details. This is what I sent. - "I am VERY disappointed with the return policy for the Kindle Fire HD. There needs to be a REASONABLE exception to the 30 day return policy, especially for instances like mine where I keep having problems with the replacements as well. I have had 3 new Kindle Fire HDs in 8 months, all with different problems. On August 27, 2013, I was told by agent Melicia W. that because of all the problems I was experiencing, I would be able to return my latest Kindle Fire HD for a pro-rated return of around 80% of the original purchase price. When I opted to take this option after thinking about it for a couple weeks, I was told I could only get a refund after the 5th replacement. I think that's absolutely ABSURD that you would make a paying customer go through a total of SIX defective Kindle Fire HDs before offering to refund their money. Obviously I want a working tablet, so I'm having a 4th Kindle Fire HD sent out. I can hardly wait to see what problems I will have with this third replacement. This product should not have so many problems, and if it does, a simple refund would be appropriate.Unhappy and fairly disgustedWithin minutes, I received another e-mail from customer service asking me to call in to speak with one of their agents so they could issue me a refund. What??? I was just told they don't issue refunds after 30 days. Seems like someone else agreed that making a paying customer go through 6 defective Kindles is a bit excessive. Each Kindle Fire HD I had came with a completely different problem. To my amazement, I provided a few details and the FULL REFUND was in my bank account the next day. EXCELLENT customer service and the right thing to do.With my experience, I would never purchase another Kindle Fire HD. I think they need to revamp the entire tablet, even though I know most people had a positive experience. With that being said, I just saw the all new Kindle Fire HDX tablets. I am considering the 8.9" version. From what I can tell, they have totally revamped these tablets. If I decide to purchase one, I know what you might be thinking, but at the very least, I know I will get EXCELLENT customer service. Thank you Amazon and thank you Jeff Bezos...

Let's start with a few disclaimers.1) The Fire HD 7 is my first Kindle Fire, though I own what became the Keyboard Kindle when the Touches were introduced, and have used it extensively for reading.2) I already own a "real Android" tablet...the Motorola XOOM 4G running Ice Cream Sandwich, so I do not need, nor did I expect, the Kindle Fire HD to be a "real" tablet.3) I also own an iPad 2, which I bought for a project at work.I bought the Kindle Fire because I wanted to be able to watch Prime Instant Video on a tablet. Simple as that. I also justified the price by promising myself I would use it while traveling to listen to music and read books (in hotel rooms and on airplanes)...and I might even buy and download a movie to enliven a long domestic flight on occasion. And, of course, for anyone who uses Amazon digital media services even a medium amount, the price of the Kindle Fire HD is right. $200 is a reasonable investment for a better Amazon Prime experience.And lets clear up the "real tablet" thing quickly too. The only reasons I can think of for Mr. Bezos calling the Kindle Fire HD "the most advanced 7 inch tablet in the world" are 1) he has never seen a Nexus 7, 2) he is not laying awake at night wondering what the wizards of Cupertino are dreaming up for the iPad Mini, or (perhaps most charitable) 3) he was simply carried away by a parent's justifiable pride at the new prodigy in the family.And lets get that straight too...though it is not a "real Android tablet" by a stretch, the Kindle Fire HD is indeed a prodigy! What it does it does brilliantly. Mr. Bezos should have rested his case when he made the "not a gadget but a service" argument. It is a brilliant argument...maybe even a winning argument...considering the depth and breadth of Amazon's digital offerings. Only Apple comes close to offering the kind of digital ecosystem Amazon has built, and their need, (whatever its source) to keep the hardware required for access to their domain at a premium price level is becoming harder and harder to justify. Amazon has it right. Put hardware access in easy reach, and let the consumers consume!So, what did they get right with the Kindle Fire HD, hardware wise?1) a brilliant screen that makes watching digital movies and tv shows a pleasure. Yes, slightly less glare, but mostly it is just a very rich screen...vibrant color, excellent detail, easy to look at. Nice!2) sound that puts any other tablet and almost all laptops in the shade. You can actually sit and listen to music on the Kindle Fire HD with some measure of pleasure. Dual stereo speakers and Dolby digital processing works. As I write here, I am listening to Alasdair Fraser and Natalie Haas's Highlander's Farewell. Fiddle and Cello. Not easy music for small speakers. The fiddle is open and detailed without strain, and the Cello has enough body to be satisfying. The sound is good enough so all my various portable speaker solutions for travel will never see the inside of my suitcase again.3) excellent wifi. I know, some reviewers are saying they see no stronger signals or faster speeds...but, for me, that is not the point. In my house we have single router and between 4 and 6 connected devices on all the time (well...not in the middle of the night...but you get the point). About 20 minutes of uninterrupted viewing is all any device in my house can manage when connected to an Amazon Instant Video stream. Then the "connecting" thingy comes on and I sit there for up to 60 seconds while it finds the stream again...and often enough I have to close the player and go back to the Resume button to get the video to continue. Yesterday I watched the whole first season of Single Handed, 270 minutes of totally uninterrupted video, on the Kindle Fire HD. Never at stutter. Never a dropped frame. Never a lost connection. Perfect. I attribute that to the quality of the wifi...probably to the device switching over to the second wifi band where there is nothing else going on in our house...and maybe a little to the improved antennas and digital signal wizardry also packed into the Fire's wifi radio. Whatever. It works. I will give you all an update after my next trip. If the Fire improves wifi reception at an airport...well then, that will say a lot!4) an overall build that says, quietly, "this is a quality product". It feels good in your hands. It feels solid. It is the right size and shape to hold easily in any position. The buttons I will get used to I am sure. (Almost...at least they are there.) In my opinion it matches the functional build quality of either my Motorola or the iPad...and the smaller size is certainly attractive for travel and easy-chair consumption.Moving then to the user experience interface...remember I am coming from unadorned Android Ice Cream Sandwich and some experience of iOS 5...well, the Fire it gets the job done. I found it easy to get around, right out of the box, and it certainly an elegant front end for the Amazon Digital Media Services. Some have said it might be easier for the beginner than either straight Android or iOS, and certainly that is correct if all you want to do is connect to Amazon, browse the web a bit, and check your email. Beyond that, I always found both Android and iOS to be pretty intuitive as well.The Email client, while it gets high marks for connectivity (Exchange means you can get email from almost any service that is not firewalled or protected by a VPN), is pretty basic. The layout is annoying in that in landscape fully half the screen is taken up by a useless list of your emails, leaving actual messages jammed into the other half. Any html message will not fit without a lot of scrolling around. This will not be my favorite way of checking email, but it is there if and when I need it.The Silk Browser has never lived up to its hype. I am not sure why. It sounds like a good idea in theory. Again, Silk will never be my browser of choice but it works. You can even access Google+, GMail, Reader, etc. if you really must check into your G-world on your Fire.The standard issue Facebook and Twitter Android clients are as good on the Fire as on anything else...and might be, for whatever reason, just a bit faster. (Or that is my impression...maybe it is that wifi thing again.)Skype is brilliant! Excellent camera and excellent wifi mean an experience at least as good as you can get on your laptop...and for a tablet that is saying much.And, of course, the Books, Music, and Video apps, as portals to the Amazon services, are of the expected quality. (I noticed some lag calling up the keyboard in the search box of the Book Store which I hope they fix, but other than that...). I will be downloading some of my music from the Cloud Player to the device for trips, but I am listening to streamed music here at home and it is perfect. As a reader, the quality of the screen makes a big difference...I won't be carrying my Keyboard Kindle on trips anymore...but then I don't read out of doors anyway.So, conclusions:No, sorry Mr. Bezos, the Kindle Fire HD 7 is not the most advanced 7 inch tablet in the world...surely the Nexus 7 still claims that title...but as a portal to the whole world of Amazon digital content it is simply brilliant. The right hardware to ensure a quality experience on all fronts. The right software to make digital consumption a pleasure. It really is a service...not a gadget.Gadget lovers (and app addicts) will still far prefer the undisguised Android experience, and there are lots of tablets out there for them. (Though I doubt we are going to see Amazon Instant Video on any of them any time soon.)The better comparison is to the iPad and any possible iPad mini. If you remember the iConcept was originally very like Amazon's current hardware/service concept (except for hardware pricing of course). Remember. iTunes. iPod. When the iPhone came out they did not even intend to allow 3rd party apps! Then the development community just stole the platform and ran away with it...and Apple had the good sense to get out of the way (well...actually...they figured out a way to make a profit off it). Even with addition of TV and Movies to the iTunes experience, over the years the digital media services aspect has taken the back seat to the hardware and to the whole iOS phenomena. Even if Apple has an iPad Mini up their sleeve for the Christmas season, I doubt they will be able, or willing, to match Amazon's hardware pricing.And, honestly, the whole closed, highly restrictive, heavily protected ecosystem of Apple's iTunes and hardware got old for me some time ago. I want to be able to consume the same digital content on whatever device I happen to be using at the moment. Amazon does this right. Apple does not. .That leaves a window for Amazon...a wide open window. They have the digital content. They have the right attitude toward consumption. Now, in the Kindle Fire HDs, they now have a world class delivery system...hardware portals that provide brilliant, easy access...priced so that almost anyone can afford one...priced, in fact, for gifting.I just got my Christmas present early.
summary: Not the best tablet, but the best Amazon experience!

reviewText: Ugh...So I've had four Kindles counting this one. I never bought a case for any of them and my children/niece broke all of the first three by dropping or stepping on them. So I ordered this reburbished Kindle. When it came, I tried to set it up but there was some type of error connecting to my amazon account. The web browswer would work but it couldn't sync with my prime account for some reason...So...I called customer service and they helped me troubleshoot it. They ended the call before I was able to make sure their advice worked and of course the same problem persisted. Next, I tried the online chat to fix it. I chatted with one person who helped me troubleshoot to no avail. They immediately transferred me to a different department without my authorization, which normally wouldn't be a big deal, but keep reading...The next person I talked to also couldn't figure out the problem and made me AGAIN do all of the same steps I just tried. It still didn't work and they AGAIN transferred me to another department.You can guess what happened next? A new person, a quick transfer. A new person, a quick transfer....Eventually, after two hours, I made it back to a person I'd already talked to. I had to give them instructions that they are not allowed to pawn me off to another department. Finally, this person gave up on troubleshooting and offered to send me another refurbished Kindle. NO THANKS! They refunded me my money eventually after I returned the product. That is how my relationship with Amazon had its first hiccup in all of my years as a member and user.Still without a solid tablet to this day as I don't like my Samsung Tab 3 either...

I won't get into too many details because there is literally hundreds of reviews talking about the features and price comparison. I'm just going to say that the screen looks great, speakers are the best ever, and it's solid.But what I will include in my review is a few opinions.1) the bigger version is better. Yeah it's the same hardware and software for the most part, but the extra screen space is really really worthwhile. If you've got *any* spare cash, please consider 8.9 over the 7.2) accessories that should be included. Amazon was great enough to include a USB cable, but that's it. No covers, bumpers, screen protect or even a charger. Yulp, not even a charger. You do get the option to bundle things at a discount when you buy this, and it's to your best interest to do so. Pick up the charger for $9.99, because when you change your mind later on, it's $19.99 separately. Also, if you consider going mobile or throwing it in your purse, consider a screen protector or cover. It will reduce the greatness of the screen slightly, but you really don't want scratches. A spare cable is also really nice if you travel a lot.3) Ads. It really urks me that you have to pay to have ads removed. This is just amazon milking a little more money from the customer base. You can find very similar tablets that match features and hardware for $199.99 that doesn't cram advertisements on your device.Overall I would not purchase this device for myself. I feel that pricing it for $199 is kind of dishonest. It cost to remove ads, it cost to add a charger, by the time you're said and done it's really closer to $225 before tax. For relatively the same hardware and features and $199 price tag, I would recommend Nook HD or Nexus 7. The only plus side is the tight integration to Amazon's electronic services. It's an alright buy for prime members, but if you don't have prime you should pass.PS, It really does have great speakers
Works fine for a 7 inch but the next time I decide to purchase it will be for the bigger model - it's a little small for web-browsing, etc

Poor tablet experience as most android features are disabled and hidden. Also, and this is a huge buzz-kill, you can't download free amazon prime content for offline viewing without paying for it as though it was not a free prime member view.Speakers are good. Screen okay. Speed a bit slow. There are much better tablets out there for the same price, only many won't work with amazon prime content.Amazon is probably afraid to release a decent prime video app for nexus 7 because no one would by their brain dead POS (point of sale) tablet.

reviewText: The Kindle Fire HD is really a joy to use. Was looking to get and have ordered the 8.9 several times not being able to decide which model to get; either the LTE or Wireless only. After reading endlessly the forums and reviews I finally decided to just get the HD since having it in my hands was a much better way to see how I would enjoy it's bigger brother.Well, I do enjoy using it and the reading is a pleasure on it. Surfing the web is reasonably responsive. Screen brightness it perfect, features are adequate. Would like it to be more easy to side-load other Android apps though. This keeps it from being five stars. Limiting the access to the Fire HD probably helps in quality control in some respects which is another thing that counters my one star downgrade. Using Silk as the browser also limits exposure since pages uses the Amazon servers as a proxy (interface and hopefully checks for Malware).Still looking now to get the 8.9 Wireless after getting my phone upgraded with a hotspot, thinking this would be a better solution for me. Then, I will have one at work (Fire HD) and one at home (8.9).Mar 2013, I cannot recommend this as a tablet. The HDfire is just gotten to slow to use. I have only 1/3 of the memory in use so this is not the issue. I can't figure it out, it ran very well the first couple of months, now it is very disappointing. It is a good reader but the lower priced one may be better if it can only be used as a reader. Don't bother thinking this can be used as a tablet.
summary: Kindle Fire HD is really a joy to use...no longer..it stalls

This is my second kindle fire hd. The first one was bought for my mom, and now I have one. I also own the Nexus 7 that was released in 2012. The Nexus was a quad core, but my biggest complaint was then occasional stuttering... and occasional manual reboots to fix that problem.The KFHD is super smooth. Never stutters or lags... even though it's only a dual core processor. that tells me that Amazon did a really good job optimizing the OS to the hardware.Overall, I find the user interface to be simple to navigate. And that's probably a good thing for most users. I'm used to having a little more control in customizing the UI. But I knew that before I purchased.The one drawback is the lack of Google Apps that I've become very familiar with. But I knew that too before I purchased. The Amazon ecosystem is very well laid out. Movies music & I do have a lot of Amazon content as well. But I do miss the apps.So where do I go from here? The Kindle Fire HD is very well made. Build quality is top notch. On the software side, it could be a five-star with just a little bit of tweaking. For those consumers not afraid of tweaking, head on over to XDA Developers website. I recommend you root the device and add the Google app such as Google Plus Google Hangouts Google Maps Google search. They can coexist with the Amazon ecosystem if you root the device. Then you basically get the best of both worlds.EDIT: 2013-07-29Just a note that my second Kindle Fire HD (16 GB) was purchased for $129 at Staples... $40 off coupon and a $30 off coupon.
summary: Very Nice Tablet. Needs Google Apps

The Kindle Fire HD is a nice improvement to it's predecessor but it still needs some work.Pros:* The screen is very sharp and crisp, not as nice as the iPad but for this price, it's pretty great.* The sound from the Dolby audio is amazing, however- having the volume up all the way is nice and loud but lower it just a little bit and the volume lowers a whole lot.* Added native email support, unseen from the original Kindle.* Syncs well with the cloud, however I haven't been able to STREAM from the cloud, if I want to watch or read something it downloads it.Cons:* The ads, $15 to remove something you paid a high amount for, even when "Special Offers" wasn't mention in the description as it is with other Kindles* The wifi isn't as great as they make it out to be, I can stay connected better than the original Kindle, but it's not "lag free"* The screen on off/power button isn't tactile at all and I have to look for it every time I want to turn it on or off* Getting out of a book is more work than it should be, it took me awhile to figure out I had to tap really fast with my index finger to bring up the menu* Going from page to page doesn't have that cool little page animation like it did in the keynote, it just slides. Not a big deal.* The carousel is more fluid than the original Kindle, but they should make another "theme" since some people, me included, find the overall UI quite clunky.* Not a whole lot of apps to chose from, and the apps in the store, not all of them are made for the Kindles size.* No wall charger, not a big deal-- I'll use one from my old Kindle.Amazon-- Nice tablet, but you really need to remove ads (for free) and give us access to the android market. Polish up your UI a bit too.Design: 4 Stars (Suffers because of non-tactile buttons and lack of rear camera)UI: 3 Stars (Could be much better)Audio Quality: 4.5 Stars (Fix volume changing so much)Screen Quality: 4 Stars (Not quite HD, and the aspect ratio isn't designed for watching movies)App Selection: 2 Stars (Obvious)Total: 3.5 Stars, I'll give it 4 stars for now, since it did just release.UPDATE:Downgraded to 3 stars. Just falls way short of my expectations, I love Amazon and will continue to shop from them. I might just return this however though, and get the Nexus 7 or wait for the iPad Mini. It's just too clunky, and half of everything you see is trying to sell you on something else. I wanted to turn the volume off on an app, and used the only tactile buttons this thing has (volume rockr) and it didn't work. Turns out most apps have their own volume controls. Some that don't even work, so the volume controls don't do anything really. Might be returning this. Going to give it a couple days.

But it's growing on me. Taking it out of the box my initial impression was how heavy it is. Then I noticed that the screen is pretty small (it measures 7 inches diagonally). I actually bought this because I've been using my Samsung Galaxy phone a lot to look at the internet, and just got tired of the small screen. I think for personal use the Fire is fine in terms of screen size, although the black frame around it seems unnecessarily wide. Web pages seem to load very slowly with the Silk browser, so I'm now using the Dolphin browser, which is faster and has Flash player capability.
