reviewText: For a few weeks I had made the decision to get a hub to be the center of most if not all my media. I had taken into consideration servers, gaming platforms, and competing media streaming devices. The most important thing for me was that it would easily integrate to my pre-existing devices: laptop, desktop, smartphone, table, and external memory device. The Roku 3, with its proprietary mobile application and the multiple channels available was able to accomplish this beyond my expectations. It is very important for the user to get familiarized with all of it's features and available channels to take full advantage of this product. To summarize,I am able to do the following with the Roku 3:Play virtually all paid streaming services (Netflix, Hulu, Spotify)MusicMoviesTVYoutube/Veoh/DailyMotion (youtube will require 3rd party channels)Stream media from my computers, phone, tablet and external hard drive (best channel in my experience is Plex)Stream live news stations (I suggest nowhere tv)Play interactive games (comes free with angry birds)These is only a summarized list of its capabilities. But once again, it is very important the user does their research on how to use the product to its full potential.Great price + Amazing Product = Happy Customer.
summary: Do your research to unlock its full potential

reviewText: I decided to look for cable alternatives when I was opening my $145 cable bill for TV and internet as I scrolled through channel after channel of PPV, Spanish language programming, and paid advertising. After doing some research on this product and Apple TV I decided on this unit. I am not heavily invested in Apple products and iTunes, plus I already subscribe to Amazon Prime which is carried on Roku.I am one of the least technical people on the planet and I had no issues setting this unit up. Between my Amazon Prime and the totally free movie on Roku I am satisfied with the movie choices. Some of the free movies do have advertising in the middle of them, but that's just like traditional TV. Although there is free programming there is A LOT of paid programming. For example Big Bang Theory is $1.99/episode on Amazon Prime but you can go to the CBS website and watch full episode reruns there for free (I was watching reruns on my DVR at a cost!) They have several news channels for free that will play back to back news stories just like traditional TV.Another big benefit is that many of the movies I look at on Roku are in HD without having to pay extra like you do with the cable companies.One of the small things I notice is that you cannot push a button, while your movie is playing, to see information about it (Title year, logline. cast etc...) like you can do with traditional cable.When I called AT&T; to cut my TV service off and the guy realized he was not going to change my mind, he offered to increase my data speed and give it to me for 1/2 off for a year so I went from a $145 cable bill to a $33 bill. For that savings amount I will definitely get used to the differences in traditional cable vs. Roku. You figure after the first month of use the Roku paid for itself in cable bill savings!Lastly, you can purchase a $10 antenna here on Amazon that will pick up most of your local channels (ABC CBS NBC, FOX PBS). I've ordered mine and should have it by next week.So my final thoughts is if you have Amazon Prime, Hulu Plus Netflix or anything like that and most of the stuff on your cable TV is crap - you will be pleasantly pleased with Roku.
summary: There Is An Adustment Period From Traditional TV

reviewText: I purchased this from a 3rd party seller who never shipped the item, but as usual - Amazon ROCKS! and refunded my money. I did end up purchasing a Roku3 from another place and honestly, I am not convinced it is worth the additional money over the XS. Here is what I posted in my review on the XS, regarding the different Roku's...The XS I purchased here was defective and I had to return it. I was initially so frustrated with Roku that I purchased a Sony digital player instead. With this XS, I spent HOURS trying to get it to update, and FOUR calls to USELESS Roku customer support for them to finally tell me to return it! They could have saved me six hours by saying that on my first call! The XS came with old firmware and would take about 20 minutes to download the 'new' software. Each and every time it would download to 100% and then restart, but it did NOT upgrade! The Roku customer support people treat you like an idiot and try every script they have to convince you it is an issue with your network and not the Roku!BUT at last I decided to give Roku another chance. We now have an XS, XD and a 3. To be honest, I see no difference between the XS and the 3 except for YouTube on the 3. The interface is exactly the same on all three boxes. The only difference between the XS and the 3 is the headphone jack in the remote and access to YouTube on the 3. I have read all the reviews saying that the 3 is so much faster, but it is not for us. But in all fairness, our internet is less than the recommended minimum. Netfilx and Amazon work VERY well on all three boxes. Hulu does NOT - we canceled Hulu because it just would not work with our internet connection. I like the XS over the XD because of the option to run a hard wire to the box instead of just wireless, although the XD with the wireless works good with Netflix, and OK with Amazon. For the money, if I have to replace the 3 I would go with the XS, and always buy from a company that has a good return policy in case you get a defective one.

reviewText: In my opinion, the Achilles' heel of the Roku line (Roku3, Roku2 XS, etc.) is its user interface. Even though the new Roku3 has an improved interface, it isn't enough to help users in navigating the 750+ channels that Roku claims to have.Roku needs to devise a user-customizable menuing system where these channels can be grouped under different categories so that finding one in hundreds won't be so difficult.In the Roku3, while channels in the Channel Store are organized using subgroups, once you place the ones you want to subscribe in "My Channels", the channels are presented in one huge, flat database. Using Roku's current interface is like using the DOS file system of 1981, where there is no provision for subdirectories (all files can only be located at the root level, and there can be no more than 512 entries). I have 99 channels in "My Channels" and I have to press the "scroll down button" 30 times in order to go through all 99 channels. In this example of 99 channels, depending on the order in which you have selected your channels, you may have to scroll up or down a maximum of 15 button presses to get to a particular channel. If "My Channels" allows subgrouping, finding channels will be much simpler.My Channels should be completely user customizable. For example, TuneIn and SHOUTcast Radio can be grouped in the "Radio" subgroup, and Cnet, Aol.on, Revision3, etc. can be grouped under "Technology". Moreover, since these are just "labels/pointers", each channel can appear in more than one sub-category, so cnet can appear under "My favorite channels" and "Technology".On the hardware front, compared to Roku2 XS, Roku3 now has the Audio In port on the remote rather than on the main unit itself. The advantage of this design is that you can plug in a pair of earphones to keep the sound to yourself while playing a game or watching a movie. The disadvantage of it is that you can't get any sound if your video monitor does not have any speakers built in, even though the HDMI cable carries both video and audio signals. I end up having to plug in my speaker cable to the remote in order to get sound, making the remote no longer "wireless". Note that this is a problem only if you connect the Roku3 to a computer monitor that does not have built-in speakers.Although all Roku's feel only lukewarm to the touch when running, do not place anything on top of the unit. It still needs to ventilate heat through its plastic case material. At one time I had a book sitting on top of it, and it became surprisingly hot.I am quite amazed that Roku only warrants its hardware for 90 days. If you use certain American Express or VISA credit card to make the purchase, the warranty gets doubled, so in the case of a Roku purchase, you'd get 180 days. My Roku2 XS has been quite reliable.
summary: Powerful and smooth, but still needs better user interface to navigate so many channels

This Roku model 3, top-of-the-line (i.e. most expensive) has ONLY a single HDMI out connector. No optical fiber cable for pristine audio, and no composite video/audio out (RCA jacks), which earlier-simpler models do have. I bought this "improved, faster" model to replace the one in our entertainment console, because it supposedly facilitates/supports the new NetFlix multi-user feature (more on that later). Useless except for a single TV with an HDMI input. We use optical (fiber optic) cable to connect to our surround-sound Sony receiver. Advantage there is that the TV can be off (for listening to Pandora music) and of course sound quality. A pure unadulterated digital signal gets delivered. And the RCA jacks, yes-now-almost-obsolete, are essential for TV EARS (a wireless headset often used by hearing impaired folks and for quiet listening/watching). So why not give granny the cutesy Roku remote with earbuds? Because when the buds are plugged in, the HDMI-to-TV audio gets muted! No one else in the room can hear. Dumb, really dumb. And what if you're a couple living in an apartment or whatever and want to watch something together without annoying neighbors and have two wireless phones? No.New TVs generally are "Smart", meaning they have streaming capability built in (no Roku needed). (And now Google Chromecast, Amazon Fire/Kindle TV, Xbox, and PlayStation stream too.) A guess is that Roku Engineering said "We can make it smaller and cheaper and call it `Improved' and hopefully stem the TV-maker's trend of eliminating the need for Roku." Marketing/Accounting/Management obviously bought that without user research and doubled the price. It's like the newer cars that are so "smart" anticipating what they think is what you want and need they eliminate user (driver) control. "Belts on, lock all doors now, lights that stay on etc."Oh yes; on the NetFlix multi-user feature: You can have more than one user (same account, same cost), each with a unique "User Profile" for their own personal "My List" (viewing preferences). Mom has her Chick Flicks, Dad his Sci-Fi, Junior Sponge Bob, and toddler Curious George. Up to now, NetFlix viewing preferences/suggestions have been co-mingled and a pain to slug through for each individual. Very cool feature, but alas, Roku 3 for me won't work. Sent it back. (Note: The Amazon Roku 3 web page mentions nothing about limited connectivity.)BTW, you'll probably find the "NetFlix Channel" the most popular by the family: Cheap, diverse and extensive content, best user interface, and quite reliable. (Other streaming providers often "hiccup", crash, and hang.) IMPORTANT! Use your computer on the NetFlix.Com website to search and pick your movie choices, which are then automatically transferred/queued to your TV "My List". Far faster, far more movie choices, and far better user interface than that funky on-TV keyboard nonsense.So why the big deal with streaming? NO COMMERCIALS! Sweet. Broadcast TV has become so laden with dumb-down advertising, and 10 commercials in a row, some the same? Give me a break. NetFlix, Amazon are worth every subscription penny; even more. I'll never watch "TV stations" again.NOTE: Streaming is for archived content, mainly. Movies, old TV series (sans commercials!),documentaries. But for real-time happenings like sports games as they happen or breaking news, keep your "Rabbit Ears" or cable or sat connection.BTW, have you noticed the ugly trend now on Internet "news" portals like Yahoo, USA Today, NY Times, Microsoft that FORCE you to watch a commercial before seeing a news clip? I click away from such a site immediately. I could care less about the latest sexy fragrance of ladies underarm deodorant. Static sidebar photos and text advertising are fine, but don't waste my time without permission. "You can skip this ad in 10, 9 . . . seconds". I skip in one, to another website. Boy I hope that forced-to-watch BS stops. Crackle tried forced commercials and they're going down the tube. (Pardon pun please.)And if you want faster (steady/reliable) streaming, chances are an "Improved-Faster" Roku probably isn't the solution. Your WiFi Internet speed/reliability IS important, and also the content provider technical quality. (Crackle, Amazon and so on whose servers often choke).
I was looking for a video recording device, and the search listed Roku. It does not record, but only gives me the same features as my smart TV already has
summary: Don't need it if you have a smart TV

I'm a veteran for media streaming players. I've been using them since they first came out and barely worked right. Long before Netflix, Amazon VOD, HBO Go, etc etc. For the last few years the market has been flooded with these devices. You would think that with so many options, someone would have gotten it right by now. I thought the Roku might be that device..The Roku has a robust menu where apps are represented as channels. The graphics are clear and vibrant. Navigating the menu is fairly strait forward, however the rabbit hole can run fairly deep with some of these apps within apps. As far as online content goes, this may be the most complete device I have tested. There are literally hundreds of channels of content available, however many of them do require subscriptions. The earbud remote is an interesting feature and does work fairly well for a private listening experience..I'm an avid video streamer. I store a very large library of movies and television shows which I have collected over many years on a file server and often stream the content to my set top box (currently a hacked apple tv 2). With no hacking solution for the apple tv 3, I decided to give the Roku 3 a shot with its 1080p resolution. The apple tv 2 is only 720p. After unboxing the Roku and setting it up I was surprised to find that a credit card was required just to make the thing work. Without an account and payment method you can't get past the activation screen. This threw up a huge red flag for me as in my experience, a device that requires a payment method generally means the maker expects you to need to use it at some point..What the Roku has in online content abilities it lacks in local network capability and codecs. The Roku has no support for the most basic video codecs like avi or mpeg and only supports mkv and mp4. The Roku can play video off a usb thumb stick, but only if it's in one of those 2 formats. The only media streamer worth mentioning available to the user is Plex (aging players such as tversity and playon are also available but not recommended). Even with Plex you are still limited by the file format restrictions. The Roku cannot transcode content streamed through plex, therefore it is on the device doing the streaming to handle the transcoding. Mkv files in particular can be very large therefore any ability to watch locally streamed content will require quite a bit of processing power..For me, lack of transcoding, support for more codecs and no native media streaming feature was a deal breaker. In my opinion, these simple and basic features were omitted in order to encourage more paid content sales..Full disclosure, I returned my Roku to amazon.

Plenty of people love this little thing and there's no shortage of rave reviews from folks who are trying to abandon cable TV. This review focuses mostly on the negatives and has two parts. The first part discusses the Roku device, its setup and programming issues and the second part covers the programming available from third parties for viewing on the Roku. Many of my comments in the second part deal with the specific streaming channels that are available (or not) and how well or how poorly they work on the Roku. These aren't the fault of the Roku, but do affect the satisfaction level associated with using the Roku quite a bit.First, a review of the Roku 3: I purchased two of these for a friend who wanted to cut the cable and later one was given to me as a gift. Two of the three Roku 3's were easy to install using a wireless connection and the third was a nightmare and took hours of troubleshooting to get it set up and working. Roku phone support was some help but didn't solve the problems I had. It took a lot of Google searches for error codes to find a procedure that would allow me to set up the third Roku. In regard to the Roku that was very difficult to get set up, I have a relatively new high speed router and the Roku is less than 4 feet away from it. The other two were installed in a two story house and the Roku units were relatively far away from the router. Once set up was accomplished, wireless reception hasn't been a problem with any of the units. However, on the third unit, I've been unable to get it to work with the Android app designed to connect to it and allow the use of a cellphone or tablet as a remote control. Though the Roku unit now has a wireless connection, the Roku unit indicates that it does not see a wireless or wired connection when I try to connect it to my Android phone. This is true though all the channels can be received on the Roku 3, so it obviously has a connection to my wireless network. In summary, there are obviously some software problems with the Roku that haven't been resolved.The Roku search mechanism for finding channels and shows is very slow and requires much punching of the remote keys from a toy keyboard on the remote. It takes forever to type something in. Much effort is needed to explore and find new shows using the Roku and the remote. Though the installation instructions didn't inform me of this, I've since been told that you can log on to your account via the internet and a computer and set up your channels and shows there much quicker. Finding movies and TV on the Roku takes much searching and some effort to set up. The computer interface is a much better option. Still, the search and review process will burn up a Saturday afternoon.Now for the second part. The criticisms that follow now are not necessarily the fault of Roku, but they do have a strong effect on the quality of the Roku 3 experience.1. Streaming Channels advertised as "free" on the Roku setup menu aren't really free. All of the so called "free" channels turned out to require an account (with your email and credit card disclosures) with automatic monthly billing that would kick in after a few days or a few movies.2. There are some relatively high quality "channels" available but there are some frustrating limitations. I have access to Amazon Prime, Hulu Plus, Netflix, HBO Go, Showtime, Cinimax and Starz. So, these are the ones I'll talk about.a. Amazon Prime works well but is providing fewer movies and TV shows every year. They have current TV series, but on some of the most recent network shows, the fee to watch a single episode was $8.00. Most of the other shows had fees in the $2.00 to $5.00 range per episode. So if you miss an episode of your favorite TV show, it can cost quite a bit to catch up using the Amazon streaming service. For missed TV shows, Hulu Plus is a much better option.b. Unlike Amazon, with Hulu Plus you can find some of the major network shows the day after they aired on the network for no additional cost)over and above the monthly fee for Hulu Plus). However, just like cable the television shows include commercials. These are usually in groups of three evenly spaced along the duration of the show being watched. Unfortunately, the commercials can be very repetitive with the same commercial being shown three times in a row for several usually four) commercial breaks during an hour long show. This makes for a pretty miserable viewing experience. Hitting the mute button only takes away some of the pain. Granted, cable TV will have more commercials, but at least they won't be the same identical commercial shown 10 times in a hour long TV show. With Hulu Plus, just like regular cable TV, you're paying for a service and yet you still have to deal with extended commercial breaks. By comparison, if you have a Tivo and cable you can record the show and skip the commercials. So, in summary, if you want to revisit the Gilligan's Island shows or a missed episode of major network TV (with commercials) you can do so using Hulu Plus and it's a much better deal than Amazon. On the upside, on Hulu Plus I have been able to find some British television series that haven't been released in America on any other channel.c. Netflix streaming works well, doesn't have commercials and is affordable, but doesn't include all of the movie library they have available on DVD. It's improving slowly and I'm told the Netflix goal is to move everyone away from the delivery of DVD disks to your mailbox.d. HBO Go, Showtime, Cinimax and Starz are not available for Roku streaming (unless you already subscribe to these channels via regular cable service). So for most who wish to "cut the cable," to reduce monthly costs the premium channels will not be available unless you have a friend or relative who is spending a fortune on cable and will share some access codes. That's a pretty large block of better quality cable programming that's missing.e. There is no Turner Classic Movie channel. There is a Warner Brothers Archive Channel (for an additional fee) which has many of the same classic movies as TCM, but there is no host to explain the movie background and note interesting trivia. In other words, there isn't the ability to live stream what TCM is showing via cable. In fact, for all the channels available on Roku, the user will need to do research on movies & TV shows and know what your looking for to pick and choose the movies and shows from a long list. For all of the Roku channels, they should offer a live stream of what is on cable at that moment in addition to the ability to go in and select individual episodes you want to watch. Without this option, the quality of the experience is much less as compared to cable TV.In summary, if you're willing to put up with these limitations, the Roku can dramatically reduce the monthly cable bill at the price of diminishing the quality of the viewing experience by about 30%. If you're in college or on a very limited budget, it's not a bad deal and it's better than nothing. The quality of the streaming channels has much room for improvement.The biggest advantage of the Roku, Apple TV and Chromecast devices is that if you're willing to put up with the limitations (multiple monthly fees & accounts, limited subtitle availability, search time to find specific programming and missing premium channels) it's the best way to pick and choose the exact cable content you want to watch. You won't be forced to purchase 80 channels you'll never watch in order to get the three you want. So a limited amount of "Cherry picking" is allowed via these devices.Finally, this isn't a very good option for grandma and grandpa. It's for someone who has access to, understands and isn't afraid of using technology and software devices. If you shut off the Grandparents cable and put a Roku in their hand, they're unlikely to be able to easily find programming they enjoy watching. The Roku remote will stay on the side table and they'll be very unhappy that they can't find Judge Judy on the TV anymore. Hope this helps somebody and my apologies to the Roku fan-boys I've just really upset.2/23/14 Update: The Roku has started locking up every other use. The picture freezes and the white LED on the face of the Roku gets bright and the Roku has to reboot. It's happening with enough frequency to cause me to avoid using it if I can.
summary: Many compromises that most reviewers ignore

reviewText: This device is the best of all the Rokus and works very well.I suggest that you get rid of your cable and use one of these (or any streaming media device) to entertain yourself. I did it years ago and wont go back. I have saver SO much money and I still get to watch what I want when I want.The Cable TV industry is broken. It is time to leave and stop paying for a service that is not worth it at all.This device will enable you to do that but you will enjoy using your Roku 3.

In the past I had a LG DVD players and used it to watch Netflix. I thought I'd try the Roku. I read the box very carefully. Nothing on the box said anything about setting up an account.OK so I went to their website and started setting up an account. Even though it plainly states, "A Roku account is free and secure." It still wants my credit card information. I already have my Netflix account so why should I have to give them my information?And if I want to chat with Roku about this, I have to give them my phone number. I know we live in a goldfish bowl. But I hate giving out personal information.I went looking at the channel selections to see what different channels cost. It says on many of the "SERVICE MAY REQUIRE ADDITIONAL FEES" Again I hate surprises. If they can't tell me up front, I'm going to return it.

Although the number of channels available (over 250) dwarfs what you can get through a streaming Blu-ray player, I encountered several issues with mine and ended up returning it.First, after initial channel selection of the most used channels (Netflix, Amazon, etc.), and setting up the required Roku account, we were unable to add any additional channels to the unit either from the Roku site or via our TV. We noticed that even with the latest firmware downloaded, Netflix videos were not quite as sharp as via a Sony Blu-ray player. We also noticed that the 'multiple user' feature ("Who's Watching?") feature of Netflix, which is supported by the Sony player, was not supported by the Roku. Finally, when we, at the instruction of Roku customer service, unplugged and plugged back in the Roku, it got hung up in a boot loop and would never reboot again despite reset. Defective unit? Maybe -- but go to the Roku forum and search for "won't boot" -- this appears to be a firmware related problem as well, so my own recommendation is at least make sure you have returns whereever you purchase this. I liked the Roku idea, and would consider trying one again after several more months of firmware upgrades have gone by.
summary: Several issues to be aware of

reviewText: We really love our Roku. We replaced local cable with it, and picked up an antenna to pickup local channels with this. We are saving on average roughly $90 per month and that's with paid subscriptions to NetFlix and HuLu. My only complaint is that the channels currently offered are foreign junk or random hit/miss short skits of hodge podge people don't really watch. Truthfully there's about a half dozen channels worth viewing (maybe this is just me). Given this I still love it! I love renting movies from VuDu and watching at home, watching gaming streams on my HD television instead of my laptop, kids have all the cartoon access they could ask for, and wife gets to watch her television shows. All of this for a FRACTION of what we were paying for local cable television. It's well worth the small investment and paid for itself the FIRST month!
summary: We love our Roku! Only few downfalls.

reviewText: I am a fan of Roku. I have owned, and still have other models. This model has few advantages over the other models but one issue that will keep me away from buying again. Since this remote works off wifi, you will eat through batteries regularly. I now have the Roku 3 for a month and have replaced the batteries three times. I was actually shocked the original batteries only lasted a few hours. We don't play games with it and only used the built in headpgone twice. I have been in contact with Roku technical service and they only explain how this unit works through wifi and it is within acceptable levels. It is not acceptable to me, I don't want to fill landfills with all these batteries. I now ask the reason for buying the Roku 3 and not other model, it is for the headphone, the processor, and YouTube. I would not recommemd this model, look at other proven models.

Purchased two of these Roku 3s, both have died in the first year. Loved it until it died, 90 day warranty is not acceptable. I spoke with Roku tech they were rude and condescending. I will not recommend Roku again.

If you're anything like me you don't like being limited. Unfortunateky Roku is the definition of limitations. For what it's worth the Roku box DOES what it's advertised to do: stream content from some of the most popular websites. You'll find out that this gets old pretty quickly. Most of the good content you still have to pay for through subscription. You can EASILY spend as much on these as you do for regular cable. I soon went looking for other options and discovered the g-box mx2.I'd compare these units but unfortunately the Roku has nothing on the mx2, it's not even a fair battle. Where the Roku is good at one thing, streaming simple content, the mx2 does literally everything else for me that the roku can't. For one the Roku is limit and cant be extended. You can't connect it to a NAS to stream, you can't install apps from the Google Play Store, you can't fully browse the web, doesn't run XBMC, and on and on. All of these things I wanted to do I discovered werent possible. Is it Roku's fault? Nope, it's my own for not doing more research before I went out and bought it. Now Ive got the mx2 and problem solved and the Roku went back to it's home where it should have stayed: Best Buy.If you're looking for very simple streaming with no bells and whistles the Roku is for you. If you're looking to do hardcore streaming or need an HTPC setup then you'll have to go for something like the g-box mx2. For the same price it's multitudes better and not limited.Hope this is useful for somebody out there. I didn't give it one star because it does what it claims it will do. but it doesn't deserve any more because this roku is pure hype. Their marketing makes you believe this thing is the holy grail of streamers when it's simply not even close.UPDATE: I need to clarify that the reason I wrote this review wasn't to point out what the Roku ISNT capable of as much as to point out that theres another device which I now own 4 of that does everything the Roku does but better and isnt limited to just streaming.
summary: Returned and got the g-box MX2 instead. Best decision ever.

reviewText: The remote control on this device seems to interfere with the other devices in my household which also use the same frequency bands.

First - I LOVE the idea... and when it works, I love my Roku player. But the programming end has serious issues. First the headset connection failed on the remote. Or it didn't fail, but it wasn't working. Roku was great about sending a replacement, but meanwhile, one of the best features that allowed me to listen to TV at night while the wife slept, was missing. This happened within the first 30 days. The second remote had a similar problem shortly after pairing, but Roku tech support sent me a button-pressing sequence that reset the remote and VOILA! Problem solved.Second - purchased online on July 31st. On December 24th, the Roku locked up following an error about the Netflix server, and didn't come back online for 3 days in spite of repeated powering off and reconnecting, etc... So, umm.... what now? We bought it for $99 and it has a 30 day warranty and that's it. Tech support may be able to help. I decide I'll try the reset... but want to give it one more try. Plug it in, and... VOILA. It works. I'm stumped... and annoyed. We like the product and the features and the cable savings, but I'm a bit peeved about the recurring loss of functionality. I'm going to start looking at the WiFi DVD players as a potential solution for the next time this happens - and meanwhile my recommendation is to buy the warranty.
summary: Buy the warranty & be prepared to reset the unit

reviewText: * Do Not Buy Seriously Flawed ROKU 3 *I have been a ROKU owner since they began offering devices in 2008 and have purchased over 8 of their media players. I've loved all of them and the company, until ROKU 3 was released.The new ROKU changed their technology to use a WiFi-Direct interface to its new remote control so it can offer a headset input, but it is flawed because it broadcasts on the same channel (2.4 or 5) that it receives on. What's worse, the WiFi signal is so strong that it jams the wireless internet signals from your wireless router to all of your other wireless devices.The result is that there will be MASSIVE interference, causing all other devices (phones, computers, Wifi to lose bandwidth and either drop the signal intermittently or fail to connect entirely.Google " Roku 3 effect on wireless" . It is an established fact. ROKU should do a recall and redesign this defective product.I strongly suggest that you select the ROKU 2 or lower devices. DO NOT BUY THE ROKU 3.Here's why I'm 100% certain the Wi-Fi Design Flaw issue is being caused by the ROKU 3.1) When I unplug the Roku3, the problem disappears.2) When I replug the Roku3 back in, the problem reappears (i.e. MASSIVE interference, causing all other devices, phones, computers, Wi-Fi to lose bandwidth and either drop the signal intermittently or fail to connect entirely).By the way, I have repeaters in my house which produces a very strong WiFi signal so there shouldn't be any problems connecting wirelessly to the Internet. The ROKU3 overwhelms the WiFi signal from all.3) I also have an original ROKU, and ROKU 1, ROKU 2, and ROKU 3. No other ROKU unit causes WiFi interference.4) The only work around is to unplug the ROKU3 when not in use, and replug it in when I need to use it.5) This is Ridiculous. ROKU needs to fix this design flaw.

Aaaargh!!!!The frustration that this thing induces is beyond acceptable!We have been using the XS model for years with absolutely no problem. Even the Roku app for smart phone works beautifully on that one. For a while, it also worked on the Roku 3 with no issues.Let me set the scene for you:We have a small wicker basket by the TV and when we are done watching on the Roku, we place the remote there, with all the other controls for the TV, Blu-Ray player, CD player, and all the other remotes that invade our lives. They are easily accessible and no one sits on them or loses them on the couch. They are all as pristine as the day we bought all those items that they make function. They are all quite a few years old.Except the Roku 3This was purchase on June of 2013 and it set up and installed as easily as the Roku XS. In no time at all, we were all a very happy family enjoying the simplicity of the Roku with the simple remote that mkes life easier.Until 3 months later.The remote stops working.We replace rechargeable batteries like crazy.There is nothing wrong with the batteries as we found out by simply removing and replacing them in other remotes.In the middle of a show the remote will quit working.In the middle of a show, the box will freeze.A search on line yielded customers complains along the same lines.I called Roku and they instructed me on how to upgrade the remote to the newer version by a series of secret commands you won't find with your Roku 3 instructions.After it cycled and paired with the base unit, it worked well... for another week.For the past few months we have been losing the ability to use the remote on a daily basis. This does not happen with Roku XS and they don't make that model anymore.Customer service was not pleasant and did not resolve the problem that, by now, should be fully aware affects these units (they can just google it)When it works, it works as it should (like previous versions) but this unit is more problematic on a daily basis than it is worth having around.It seems to get hotter than the XS as well.We kept thinking it is the remote, but I think it is the unit itself because randomly it will just reboot itself in the middle of a program.The best feature of this unit is the headphone jack to watch in silence while the household is sleeping, but now even the headphones stopped working and even the replacement headphones are dead.As soon as I find a refurbished XS online I am making the switch. It is appalling that they won't fix these units when customers tell them there is a problem with them and the problem is the same across the board.This is their shinny new flagship model and, in our case, it has been a failure.My advice if you purchase one is to be aware of the 90 day warranty and put this thing through its paces morning, noon, and night because otherwise, you are stuck with the frustration and your wallet is a lot lighter. If you don't care if the unit has a headphone jack in the remote, I strongly recommend the XS as a refurbished unit. Our experience with that unit has been flawless for the past few years and it is highly recommended.Good luck and I hope this review helps you make a decision.

I bought this back in August and now it does not work. I am well past the amazon return time frame. The remote has had connection issues. The WIFI has had connection issues on the device, and at times it freezes up. But now I am unable to do anything with it.
summary: Does not work after a few months

reviewText: I have had this Roku for about 5 months. Well to be fair I have had 3, 2 died and I am on my 3rd. One thing in Roku's favor is their customer service is pretty good. Sure it's your typical person with a checklist and if you ask something off of it they are completely lost but isn't that the standard theses days?ProsStreams well.Nice but slightly cheap felling design.Easy setup.Lots of "channels".App storage is expandableExternal playback is native through USBWifi signal strength isn't the creates but it is very stable which is actually even more important.ConsTotally underpowered. Price is double even triple on dated hardware and better spec'd TV sticks with less uses for the device.remote is a little slow to respond. So far I haven't found an air mouse to replace itLots of "channels". Yes, the same thing I listed as a pro. Why? Because let's be honest, the vast majority of the content for the Roku series is crap. It's kind of like Roku doesn't bother to check the content they place. Quantity over qualityRidiculous prices for the paid appsFails miserably for even casual gaming.Headphone jack on the remote wasn't a feature I planned on using so it didn't influence my rating but the sound quality wasn't the greatest even with some high end headphones including Bose OE2 and Beats Solos.The device performs as advertised. The cons I have don't really outweigh that it does stream well, which is what it should do. The 1 star off is because I did have a couple fail but customer service was quick to respond/handle the issues and that they do advertise it for gaming and it fails there. Also even with the remote, there is just no real justification for the low hardware specs versus the price. I would have knocked of more stars except it does stream well despite the technical shortcomings.I would recommend the newer Roku Stick before the 3 or 2. For the price look into some of the Android streaming set top boxes for hardware that is far superior for the same price and gives you a lot more functionality. If you have a few extra dollar of disposable income and only want a streamer then the Roku 3 is a good deal.

Having two Roku 2 units, I really like Rokus. The Roku 3 remote earphone option was my main reason for buying this one -- for use with my noisy exercise equipment. It replaces my on-the-ear wireless headphones, and lets me use more comfortable in-the-ear options.ONE THING: Roku 3, unlike earlier models, works only with an HDTV. I travel with a Roku 2 and can use it on *any* TV.If you use only HDTVs, the Roku 3 cant' be beat!

Purchase this because you can watch foreign movies and shows, so many channels. She love the Roku because it's easier for her to operate than a computer. Plus it makes a great addition to her TV.A few issue I saw:The device is small and light, I notice they added some weight but it wasn't enough to keep it on the counter if the HDMI cable is pulling. But a few double sided velco tape works wonder.The quality control needs to be better. The Ethernet port was a bit crooked, not a big deal to me but some people might think otherwise.I wish there was a way to program the Roku remote to work with the TV volume control or include the feature in future Roku.
summary: Best gift ever for my mother.

After the reset, the remote would not work, so the product isn't useable at all.My original 3 year old Roku still works fine. reviewText: Wow, I just love the Roku... have had them since they first came out, and they keep getting better and better... great value for the money.

After four hours on tech support with Roku and several emails written by support personnel who evidently kept no notes, a senior tech finally revealed that the Roku 3 outputs only Dolby Digital Plus and supports no other 5.1/7.1 formats over its HDMI connection.Make sure your receiver/TV supports Dolby Digital Plus before buying this product or be sure you are satisfied with stereo output. (Of course your receiver may be able to simulate 5.1 from Roku stereo output, but that's not what one would hope for.) I also found that if I changed audio modes on my Denon receiver, all audio was lost until I turned the receiver off and back on. I've never experienced this problem with another audio/video source (tuner, TV, DVD or blu-ray player).In addition, Netflix over the Roku consistently started out with a blurry picture, but that it would clear up in a minute or so. After that the picture was fine.Roku needs to make it explicit that the Roku 3 only supports Dolby Digital Plus. I'm sending it back.

The box is nice but not much more than a way to get Netflix on your TV if it is not internet capable. There are some games but this is not a game system at all. I would recommend you buy a B-Ray player with internet abilities and save your money.
summary: It was a cool idea some friends mentioned but pretty limited.

reviewText: Pros1) Pretty GUI, very responsive, and customizable2) USB Port to play files without the need to stream from PC3) Tons of content to choose fromCons1) If you have Xfinity Cable aka Comcast, no HBO GO!2) The included ear buds maybe the worse ones I've ever heard, although the remote works with any headphones.Overall happy with the product, but I'm very upset I have no HBO GO in my bedroom, its one of the main reasons I bought it. Hopefully Comcast starts to support Roku soon.

Does your smart TV constantly freeze or buffer every time you watch Netflix or MLB.TV? If so, it's because the apps built into the TV are a worthless waste of RAM. The Roku 3 solves that issue.In my case, the MLB.TV app on my TV was a festering cyst, with a playback constantly plagued by stuttering, buffering, freezing, and skipping. By contrast, MLB.TV through the Roku 3 is a hi-def stream dream.The only reason I didn't give this device 5 stars is because Roku has purposely crippled the Roku 3 with a couple of high-profile shortcomings.The Roku 3 WILL NOT let you stream programs on Hulu for free. It DOES support HuluPlus, but you have to pay a monthly fee for that. No free Hulu for you! You want to watch free Hulu, the Roku 3 no can do.Also, no YouTube. You'll have to get all tech-geeky on its apps, and search for, install, and configure one of the technical workarounds to watch YouTube via the Roku. Not a tech-geek? No YouTube for you!These two frustrating omissions from an otherwise decent product peg the Roku 3 barely above "meh" on the likeability scale.
summary: Beats native apps on a smart TV, but still meh

reviewText: This works so much better than my Blue Ray player for streaming video that I wish I had gotten one a long time ago. It's simple to set-up and easy to use. I love the fact that it use an RF remote so that I don't have to point it at the device and the earphone plug is a definite plus because I can now actually understand the dialogue in a movie without blowing the walls down with the volume.Everybody needs one!

I am separating the installation of the Roku 3 in 2 parts:1- I did not know that a credit card was required to activate the account since i already had accounts with Netflex and Amazon. You definitely have to have a computer, ipad or iphone to activate the account. I spent hours trying to get the Roku operational even after i entered the phrase on my computer that was displayed on the TV. Terrible setup. Roku should spent more time writing proper installation instructions and less time trying to sell me something.2- The hardware works good after setup. It is compact and connects me quickly to my Web accounts.The novice will have a difficult time doing the installation.
Chromecase is Googles answer to AppleTV. For the PC user this might be a good alternative. I wasn't impressed enough to continue using it.

Chromecast is a bit more exciting in theory than it is in practice.Pros:- Very easy installation as long as your TV has available HDMI & USB Ports- Android & iOS apps work well to configure and cast media to the TV- Pretty seamless operation once configured and on-lineCons:- HD picture quality from HBOGo or Youtube is sub-par compared to cable or roku broadcasts- Occasionally stops playing and requires restart from the app (even while showing full strength Wireless connection)- PC interface not as slick as mobile device, HBO broadcast shown on PC & TV simultaneously, doubling the bandwidth needThe first Chromecast I bought died after a week of use. First the audio was distorted, then it would just boot to a black screen. After contacting google support and jumping through a number of hoops, I was sent a replacement. It has worked well since it was installed.Issues aside, I think the utility of this device is excellent and bridges the gap between PC's/Mobile and my TV. Looking forward to seeing what improvements come in the future.
summary: Really cool but needs some improvement

reviewText: Chromecast is a neat idea but at this time that is all it is. Without support for more apps it has extremely limited use. You might as well pay the extra money and buy a Roku or Apple TV which have a full feature set. The only reason i'm giving two stars is that the device itself is neat and works decently from a technical perspective.
summary: Neat idea, without more apps somewhat useless.

reviewText: Does very little, but does it very well!If you want netflix on a TV without using other devices this is it! Will also mirror a web browser for presentations.

Easy way to stream Netflix and Youtube from my smart devices. Seems to stream in better quality than my apple tv does and is vastly cheaper. Hopefully with the release of the SDK more apps will be able to make use of the device.

I am impressed by the performance over my wifi network. I have tried the chromecast browser extension on both my chromebook and macbook. Some services like youtube, hulu plus and netflix offer direct support that is high quality. I have tried youtube and could see the difference. (I don't have netflix or hulu plus at this time.) I have also tried casting a full screen browser window of an Amazon Prime video. Amazon Prime videos streaming doesn't directly support the chromecast (yet), but the chromecast browser plugin works well. The color is a bit different and there is some latency between my computer's screen and the chromecast. But the quality is still decent and I have seen no stuttering. If and when amazon prime offers native support for the chromecast, I am sure it will be much better. One limitation to be aware of is that audio from video sources that require plugins like silverlight does not come through. So far this is not a big deal for me.
summary: Great device for streaming content to TV.

reviewText: I bought one, then I bought two more. I now have 3 Chromecasts in the home and love it. I used to be a very casual Netflix watcher, but now I watch Netflix and YouTube all the time while at home. It's so simple and now just reflex to be on my smartphone and instead of watching YouTube videos on my phone, I kick it over to my 47" TV without hesitation. Netflix streams great all the way in the living room, away from the router's strongest Wifi signal area. I highly recommend it. Set up has been a snap with all three.
summary: Chromecast is an excellent device!! I now have 3 in the home, family love it!

reviewText: I have an older flat screen tv in my sewing studio. It does not have wifi and I wanted the chromecast player installed permanently to watch YouTube videos with my Ipad. It works quite well for this purpose. It is a different concept from the Roku, I feel it is well worth the cost. The lack of good instructions keeps this a four star rating.
I like it, I don't love it. It currently only has Netflix and Hulu for watching videos. If Amazon Video gets on board, I'll be set.
summary: Good, but it needs time to develop more apps

reviewText: i like the idea of chromecast. it works well with netflix. nice for movie night with the kids. but as far as i know the uses are limited. you can't use on some random website. only established, contracted sites like netflix. admittedly, i could be wrong. as i am not the most tech savvy person -- there may very well be a way to use with other websites that i haven't figured out yet.

Initial setup was a breeze, and once setup via wifi, I was able to connect with a wired PC too, which was a pleasant surprise. Using a third party application, you can stream pretty much any video format, which is nice for someone that doesn't want or can't have the extra cables running to the TV.
summary: Very easy to set up, and can stream virtually any format...

reviewText: I own 2 of the chromecast devices. the concept and the supposed ease of use are great, your TV becomes an extension of your chrome browser which means that everything thats on the internet could be viewed on your TV.The problem is that device has a lot of issues staying connected on the network when used on the chrome browser and it messes up the wifi connection for all the devices in my experience this happens only if you cast from your chrome browser and not if you cast the few [but expending number of]apps available for the phone and tablet. This issue renders it quite impractical for chrome browser streaming but the growing number of app with casting ability are making this less of niche device and increasingly viable streaming option from phone/tablet to the home theater system.

I purchased a Chromecast HDMI Streaming Media Player as I don;t have cable TV, but I do have WiFi internet.I wanted to be able to watch Netflix on my basement tv ( which was only picking up the basic TV stations, ABC, CBS, PBS, etc.I hate watching adverts and prefer to choose my own uninterrupted programs.Setting up the device is a little tricky!Step 1. Plug it in to the HDMI slot on the TV. No problem there. I had a slot and I used the supplied short extension HDMI (about 4") to connect it. Look carefully at the advert - in the small print off to one side they mention that you need a power cord. They actually supply a plug-in power pack that you need to plug into the Chromecast device. Not a problem really, but make sure that you have a spare outlet.Step 2. Switch on the TV and go though the modes until you find the HDMI channel you plugged the device into. It displays nice pictures to look at when you find it. Again, easy enough.Step 3. This is where it gets interesting. Make sure that you have a computer, phone, etc that is listed in the small print in the advert:Supported Operating SystemsAndroid 2.3 and higheriOS 6 and higherWindows 7 and higherMac OS 10.7 and higherChrome OS (Chromebook Pixel, additional Chromebooks coming soon).Be aware that if you don't have WiFi, Windows 7 on your computer, or the correct Operating System on your phone, it won't set up!I went to the google.com/chromecast/setup on my WiFi computer with Windows 7 and was able to get through the first step, getting it to find and activate the device plugged into the TV. I think that this is where a lot of people think that they have completed the setup and think that the device is not working.What I didn't notice initially was that a second window opens up after a short while to allow you to download the program that sets up the computer to put the little Chromecast App onto your computer or other device. It was hiding BEHIND the Chromecast setup window! Once you find this and enable it you can use the device successfully - -for the listed places, like Netflix, etc. Again very carefully read the list of what the device can do.What it DID NOT DO!I tried adding it to my Motorola Admiral cell phone, which has the Android OS 2.3, but it didn't want to let me Accept the App - just washed out the screen and froze up. After a lot of playing with it I found a message that said that the device is not currently able to work on my version of the Android 2.3 Operating System! So, I'm not able to use my phone to control the device. If you have a lower end phone like me then you may have an issue.Having said all that.IT DOES WORK WELL at putting Netflix, etc on my TV. I can use the computer to do other things whilst the program plays, but I have to go back to the computer to control the program, stop, pause, etc. I'm happy that it does what I purchased it for. Picture quality and sound were excellent on my very high speed internet connection.You can name the device and then you could actually put one on different WiFi TVs and send different programs to each TV of necessary.If you have Cable or Sat TV it would not be much use to you, unless you want to view stuff from your computer or cell phone, but it does have a use if you do a lot of Internet viewing.Go the the Google Chromecast webpages and you'll find the answers to most of the problems you may have setting it up, and also what it will and will not work with at the current time.
summary: Read the small print! THIS REVIEW MAY HELP YOU

reviewText: I read about this, and waited for it to be out for a couple of months to see what others were saying about it. Finally, after it had been out for a couple of months, and I read many reviews, I decided to buy one. For $35, I felt it would be a decent gamble if it worked, and little lost if it didn't.It arrived when I expected it to, and setup took only about five minutes, with much of the time required to get the device out of the box and physically connect it to my television, and power it up. As a Netflix subscriber, I wanted a means to watch videos on my television in the bedroom, and this worked great. It takes only seconds to switch the video from my iphone to the chromcast, and the controls remain on my iphone. We have also used a tablet running android to play vidoes through this, and that works well also. Basically, if you can turn on a computer and connect it to a wireless network, you can handle this device. We have watched many movies with this, and some television shows off of Netflix, and we have had no issues with connectivity with the device during playback. I have a wireless N router, and highspeed cable broadband (10 - 20 MBS). Once you start the streaming to the device, you can turn off your device, as the streaming will continue straight from the wifi to the Chromecast Player.I am only giving this four stars, as I feel it should do more, as, right now it is limited to Netflix, Google Play, and a few others that I don't use. I hope to see the apps to increase in the future, however, this is cheaper than a Roku device, and accomplishes what it says it will do.I expect significant improvements on this device over the next few months, possibly a next generation out within six months. But, for less than the price of movie tickets for a family of four, and if you need a means of streaming videos to your television set, this is a great device. And you don't need to be a computer scientist, or build rockets for NASA to set it up. A television with an HDMI connection, a wireless router that you can connect it to, and a computer, smartphone, or other device to control the device with.
summary: Great idea, but would like more apps available for it...

reviewText: I was a little hesitant to buy this after reading some reviews, but since I realized the negative ones were probably because the people were novices, or frankly, expecting more than they should, I decided to take a chance. So glad I did! My main purpose for a Chromecast, was the ability to watch Netflix on my TV, and it does this very well. I cast Netflix from my Samsung Galaxy Note II smartphone, and it works as it should. It was very easy to set up, and connect with my home network. Now I'm even happier with it, since Google has added more applications to work with Chromecast. For the money you just can't beat it!

Not WIRELESS HDMI, you can only stream apps, which limits the use. Everything is also still in beta including most importantly Chrome browser.Rumors say soon we should be able to stream our whole screen instead of just an app.Speed is okay, slightly lag input as expected. Uses Router's Wifi network to connect and issue commands. Big problem is it only accepts 2.4GHz, no 5GHz. Fortunately my Asus AC66U dual band lets me sign onto 5GHz on phone, and control the Chromecast on the 2.4GHz signal.P.S. You still have to switch your TV's input every time so you can't ditch the remote completely, not quite a Smart TV alike, but neither the price.
Performs as promised. Shipped quickly, Updated already by Google to add access to other streaming content. Simple to use with your tablet or laptop interface. Google scores again!
Simple and easy to use. Nice product with no bells and whistles. Can't beat it for the price. Size is great..

This device works sporadically at best. About 80% of the time I have to disable something or reinstall something, or it just never works at all.I often sit there and stare at my TV with the lovely Chomecast wallpapers up, and my laptop screams 'Device not found? 'This product should still be in Beta. It is not ready for mass consumption.
summary: Device not found? Yes = about 80% of the time.

reviewText: This is a great device to allow one to use Netflix and other streaming services from any HDMI-capable TV in your house. We use it with Google Chrome (from laptop computers) and the iPad app, and both work great. Definitely a great device at a great price.
summary: Streaming Video to Any TV in the House

reviewText: This is probably just the first generation. Worth a try for the price and 3 months of neflix thrown in.
Using with an ipad, been watching youtube videos and browsing the web. Hooks up on an HDMI port on the tv, the USB port isn't working to supply power. So I have to use the power cord

works fine with netflix and youtube, but most tvs already have those apps preinstalled (smart tv) nowadays. needs to work with more apps to become indispensable. good value if you dont have smart tv i guess.
works great easy to set up I watch net flix from my cell phone. It has many uses and works great. don't know what I would do with out it.

Works like a charm. Really easy to set up and configure with WLAN. However, at time the audio wont stream, so I have had to disconnect and connect again (might be my wifi??).Other than that, I am really pleased with the product.

4 STARS IF USED WITH NETFLIX, ETC ONLY. I.e. ONLINE STREAMED MEDIA. 0 STARS IF YOU WANTED TO BE ABLE TO STREAM YOUR STORED MOVIE MP4 FILES FROM A HDD CONNECTED TO YOUR WIRELESS MODEM. THAT WOULD BE COOL AND, BELIEVE ME, IT IS COMING. THE ONE WHO FIRST MAKES THIS ITEM WILL MAKE A FORTUNE. IT IS NOT ILLEGAL TO HAVE DVDs & BLURAYS IN MP4 FILE FORMAT. IT IS MY BELIEF THAT GOOGLE IS A BRILLIANTLY RUN COMPANY & THAT THIS IDEA IS IN THIS CHROMECAST PRODUCT'S FUTURE. THE FIRST TO DO THIS WILL RULE.

reviewText: Buy a roku instead. You need a powerful computer to mirror most content and does not support silverlight / amazon prime properly.If all you want to do is watch youtube videos its fine.

Cheap $35 gadget and works with Youtube and Netflix apps. But the connectivity is crappy and many times I have to reconnect. Hope we get a firmware upgrade soon, and with out it it is not meant for primetime.
summary: Great idea but not for prime time

reviewText: I know that most folks bash Apple products, but Apple TV blows this thing away. Just the fact that this has to be used with a computer or other hand held device is a deal breaker for me. I would much rather spend the extra $63 dollars for an Apple TV with a remote, which is much easier to setup and more intuitive than Google Chromcast. Plus you can use Apple TV with Hulu plus, without having your laptop turned on. Spend the extra money for an Apple TV, you will be much happier!
summary: Not User Friendly compared to Apple TV

reviewText: I love this product and for the price it's perfect. Allows you access to your YouTube account among other things and brings it to your tv. If your tv is not capable of viewing YouTube already, then this is a great little device for the price. Only downside I find is that A) the unit runs very hot, and B) you cannot turn it off other than by unplugging it. I did check into the heat issue, and it seems to be normal and so far I have had no issues leaving mine plugged in all the time. I think it's safe, but wow does it seem hot for such a little device. If you don't have a smart tv with these features, then this is a very cheap option to bring these features to your tv.
summary: Great product, great price, but runs hot when in use

reviewText: I tested this out recently. Pros: I like the size and it work fine. It does not work with Amazon Prime video streaming service and some other online streaming services.However for the price, I thought I give it a try.I have a Netgear Push to TV adapter better. (Word of caution your laptop needs to have intel WiDi = "Wireless Display" capability and not all laptops have this capability = so if you have an AMD processor it won't work). However if you do have Intel Widl capability, then the Netgear Push to TV adapter is better fit.). .

Its ok as it streams Youtube videos easily...unfortunately very limited use other than what this device offer...pretty much just use it to stream Youtube as I dont have or use netflix. For what its worth...I think Roku is still better (its just they dont stream Youtube anymore)

I've been using Chromecast for a couple of weeks now with mixed results. For example, "casting" a web page containing video of our pastor's sermon from a week ago resulted in stuttering video and audio and dropped "casts" so many times today that we gave up and just watched it on the laptop.On the other hand, using the Chromecast button to watch TV episodes via Netflix and miscellaneous videos via YouTube has been quite successful. So we're still making up our minds whether this gadget will have a permanent place in our TV watching.We also will need to have our Harmony remote reprogrammed so we can quickly navigate to HDMI 2. Right now that involves switching to the "laptop/PC" preprogrammed setting on the Harmony, then finding the separate TV remote in order to select HDMI 2. So for us, being technologically un-savvy when it comes to Harmony programming, that will be an extra expense, since it's annoying to keep that separate TV remote around.It's kind of annoying to have a separate power cord hanging down the front of our entertainment center. There's no way to move the entertainment center away from the wall to slip the cord behind (the thing weighs several hundred pounds). I know, small potatoes when it comes to complaints! Overall, for $35, it seems like a good value for the money, as long as we keep the Netflix membership.Speaking of Netflix membership, I was under the impression when I ordered the Chromecast that it came with 3 months of free Netflix membership. I was supposed to get a confirmation email along with the "your order has shipped!" email. It never came. So I called Amazon.com today and, after 35 minutes on the phone with a customer service rep, was informed that I had missed the deadline for that promotion by four days. Yet it was still being advertised in various places long after. Irritating, but my own fault for not reading the fine print. Buyer beware!UPDATE: I brought my Chromecast to a Hilton hotel in Denver, CO, and plugged it into the back of the LG TV in HDMI 1. I then spent half an hour on the phone with the hotel chain's Internet tech support, trying to get the Chromecast and my laptop to recognize each other. But because you have to jump through some hoops when you log on to the hotel's wi-fi, and those hoops can't be jumped through by the Chromecast, there was no way to get the Chromecast and the laptop to be on the same wavelength, so to speak. We got them both online, but one couldn't see the other because tech support had to manually get the Chromecast online using its MAC ID (which has nothing to do with being on either a MAC or a PC, I found out). So don't expect to use your Chromecast in hotel TVs, unless you're using a wi-fi network that demands absolutely nothing in the way of a browser login.

I was given this device as a gift for Christmas. This is NOT an easy device to set up for those of us that don't have all the latest tech in our homes. You may find that the ONLY devise you have that will be compatible with Chromecast is your cell phone. Do you really want to be tethered to your cell phone to watch Netflix or other streaming media?This is definitely the bleeding edge of technology. Decide before you buy it how much you're willing to bleed.Update 2014-01-08I have now installed the device successfully, first using my Android Cell phone and then using a Samsung tablet. The Netflix picture is very good and much better than the Roku streaming player I used before. Pandora works well using the tablet to control it.So, my conclusion at this point is that the Chromecast is worth the price and have increased my rating from 1 to 3 stars.You should still be aware that the device you intend to use to control it must, itself, be connected to the internet via wi-fi (my main computer is plugged directly to the router by cable and therefor does not qualify). If the device is a Windows devise, it must be running Windows 7 or later. (My notebook computer has Wi-fi but runs XP, so it doesn't work).

I was more than excited to get my Chromecast. It was back ordered, and then Amazon got it to me more than a month sooner than expected. Nice job Amazon. My entire hope for this device was to drop my subscription for HuluPlus and just use my laptop to cast episodes full screen. Turns out my 2006 Macbook Core two duo running Snow Leopard can't really cut it. Later I find Chromecast wants OSX 10.7 or better, which I cannot install on my machine (not a criticism of Google. I probably need to start paying closer attention to system requirements with my decrepit computers). However, my 2008 iMac with a faster processor running the same OS casts perfectly, so it's clear casting is processor intensive. I usually get annoyed when folks post bad reviews for entirely non-product related flaws, so no stars off for this issue.Set up was a snap, even in a non supported OS! It was a strange procedure of connecting to a wifi network generated by the Chromecast itself and then setting it up. Then I was instructed to disconnect from that and go back to my house's WAN for normal use. I'm wondering just how possible it might be hack my Chromecast and gain access to my house WAN with this unsecured signal from the device (the Chromecast stores the WEP key). Minus a star.The Chromecast app in iOS works great. It's a joy to be able to share YouTube videos with my wife without having to hold my iPhone between us. I don't have anything up in GooglePlay so I can't comment on that, and we don't subscribe to Netlfix. My other great hope is Google will come through on their statement to produce/host more apps to cast more media from other sources.

The Google Chromecast HDMI Streaming Media Player is an inexpensive alternative to units made my Roku and Western Digital. The savings is not worth the additional effort required for EVERY use. All viewing selections must be made independently on a PC as opposed to the other streaming video players that have remote input units.

For some reason this device creates a separate wifi network, to which my Nexus device has to connect to stream the video.I could only manage to watch one video at a time before having to have to turn of wifi on my nexus and turning it back on. Otherwise the second video would not play. Same thing on all 4 chromecasts that I own.Faulty architecture, poor implementation. Device constantly blinking, thus creating an annoying light-effect during videos.Get a Roku instead, it's the only device that performs without hiccups in my opinion.

Good to be able to watch you tube videos on the television, but other than that it doesn't do a good job with Netflix or handle Amazon Prime. And one must have a Chrome browser computer, Android phone or tablet hooked up to Wi-Fi to make it work.
summary: ok for You Tube, but unless you have a google phone or chrome browser it is worthless

reviewText: Got this to try. I have a TV in the bedroom with a spare HDMI input and figured for $35 bucks what do I have to loose. I bought it on impulse and didn't do a lot of research. I figured it would work mostly like the roku with fewer available apps and controlled via smartphone/tablet. That looked cool, and would allow me to surf in bed without reading glasses for my tablet!It does not do that...on an android tablet. Android browser support is coming...someday.I'll keep playing with it. Maybe Google will update it some day to be more useful.Pro: Youtube (still not available on Roku)Cons: Does not do what it says. No real advantage over Roku (other than Youtube). No remote, Not very many apps/channels.Edit: I carefully re-watched the video's and they technically never say or show web browsing from an android device, but I still feel like it is almost inconceivable that they do not have this working. Chromecast didn't come out yesterday. There are some third party solutions, so it's technically possible.

reviewText: I am an appleTV user, I though this might complement my setup essentially for youtube clips. Installation was ok but clunky and counterintuitive, I had to install using my MacBook Pro since it wouldn't install with my MacPro (computer has to be within 20 feet of TV) also it wouldn't connect to the 5 GHz band of my router, only the 2.4, oh well. reviewText: Although this device is still in it's infancy I see limitless potential in the future for thiis little dongle. Google has really outdone themselves this time especially with the price point.The purchase of this gadget is really a no brainer if you purchased this with 3 months of free Netflix. With Netflix running $8 a month this unit essentially is only selling for $11. For what it can do and what it can potentially do in the future, this $11 investment is very miniscule. You'd spend just as much or more on 2 trips to Starbucks, why not put that towards something you can use for much longer?Being able to control YouTube and Netflix with nothing but your TV, Chromecast, Android device and an internet connection is such a convenience, in my opinion. I can't wait until there are more features. The ability to sling the content on your computer from the Chrome browser definitely opens things a bit. With continued support from Google and 3rd party developers, I see a very bright future for this little device.There aren't very many cons about this device. Only cons I can think about relate to the limit 3rd party support it currently has....or lack of, but that's something that will definitely be remedied in due time. It is a very new product.In the past I've used my PS3 to stream media, to connect to Netflix or YouTube but it could be troublesome to navigate with just the on screen keyboard and UI. With this you have all of the control with a very familiar setting that is your Android phone, Android tablet, PC, or iPhone.When you purchase this item it comes with everything you'll need. The device itself, an HDMI extender, and a powered USB cable to power the device itself if your HDMI port is not powered. I guess the only thing you'll need is a TV with an HDMI port. Good thing is that most people who have a TV, do.I think everyone should get one just to experience the convenience and fun factor fo this great media doo-hickey.
summary: Great Media device with limitless possibilities!

reviewText: Best thing about this is its price compared to the Roku and AppleTV. But, all it runs is Netflix, Youtube, and your Google Play stuff. That's it! That's all it does! You like Amazon Prime video? Too bad! Hulu Plus subscriber? Go hang!Also, while the device itself is famously tiny, it still requires a power cord which largely negates the convenience factor.If all you subscribe to is Netflix and you never buy or rent video from the site you are currently browsing, and if you never plan on ever getting Amazon Prime either, and you have no interest in the vast channel line-up of the Roku, then sure, I guess buy this and save a few bucks... otherwise, go for the Roku 3 and never look back.UPDATE: despite several tries at rebooting our Android phobe and uninstalling and reinstalling Google Play, there is simply no way we can stream movies from Google Play to the chromecast, despite being on the same wifi network. The "cast" button simply does not appear in the app, and nothing will bring it up. It should be noted that the Roku is not limited by a failure on a phone/tablet app since all its apps are stored internally and does not require a smartphone or tablet whatsoever. Anyway, the Chromecast has been an unmitigated disappointment, and we regret the purchase.
Everything works really well since day 1 and I just ordered another one for a 2nd tv. I love it!
summary: Cheap working product. I just ordered a second one for another tv.

reviewText: I love Google, and I am a software developer by trade, so I'm not completely ignorant of technology. I was excited about this product because it is inexpensive, it is praised for it's "ease of setup", and it's a good concept.So I plugged it into my girlfriend's TV, downloaded the Chromecast Android app to my Sony Xperia Z Ultra and proceeded to start the 'extremely easy setup'. I get "We could not communicate with your Chromecast." Then I go to a help screen that talks about disabling access point isolation, ensuring universal plug and play is setup on your router, and .net3.5 framework is installed on your computer. Fine, my girlfriend has Xfinity, and her router is not configured exactly the way Chromecast likes.Then I take it back to my house, and go through setup on my own network. I use CenturyLink for broadband, and a completely different router than my girlfriend. Same Error! Just how many routers does this thing work with? There is definitely no "EASE OF SETUP" here! I'm fiddling around with the uPNP settings on my router, I can't find ANYTHING that resembles "access point isolation", and all of the Google help tells me to go to my router instructions - that's not helpful!I think the marketing people have finally caught up to the technology people at Google, and are trying to convince us that their crappy product does something useful, but so far, I don't see it. Lost a lot of respect for Google with this debacle.

I really really really wanted this to work. It does work ok when I am just using chromecast, but when I am surfing the web anywhere else in the house, the wireless is totally screwed up now on my home network. I have to reboot my laptop every time I want to surf the web if the chromecast is plugged in, and most times I have to reset my wireless router. Kind of a joke if you ask me.

Because of the reviews I bought the Chromecast. I live in Australia and I was hoping to stream from my NAS. At least I was expecting to be able to use it to get US channels. I have an Apple TV, if you think that Apple is restrictive, well... Google is far worse.The Chromecast updates without asking. You just connected it on your wifi, sorry too late to root it.The DNS are hardcoded, you can forget US-block and Netflix / Hulu if you are not living in the US.At least, I could stream from my NAS? My network wifi and same laptop can support live tv streaming from my hdhomerun via windows media center, so it is not a weak network issue.I bought mine a few minutes after the announcement and had not thought through one obvious drawback. If you don't have HDMI pass-through on you stereo receiver, think through your audio setup. You may need an adapter or have to send audio through your TV, maybe have to change your universal remote settings, etc. If you have a new-ish tv this is not such a headache for Netflix from your phone, as it uses hdmi control and can adjust the tv's volume from there. I hooked mine up to that and used usb from my xbox to power it (powers even when xbox is off).All the marketing and demos say you have to be on the same "wifi network" as the chromecast to use it. You just have to be on the same network and subnet, not connected through the same access point. Might only matter for a few readers, but I can use this from devices attached to the network via the same access point, a different one on the same network, ethernet or MOCA bridge.Set up is easy, but changing your setup is not. Gets into your registry settings the first time through and it is hard to make it try again from the pc.Bottom line - if you want to be an early adopter and wait for features and upgrades, get one of these. Bottom line up front: most people will be better off buying aRoku 3 Streaming Media Player.The big selling point for the Chromecast was the fact that you could stream YouTube content to your television. Roku never had this functionality, instead they would have the user install less-than-reliable "private"/third-party channels to get it. Well, in mid-December 2013, Roku released a new, official YouTube channel that replicates the YouTube-streaming feature of the Chromecast on the Roku 3. YouTube channels for other Roku devices will be released in 2014, although they will not work on Roku models introduced before 2011. Chromecast's "killer app" seems to have been killed itself.That being said, the Chromecast is a perfectly adequate device if you manage your expectations a bit. It works with a very limited number of services, although more are being added. You have to control it from another device, like an iPad or Android tablet (and even then, it works with a subset of the various versions out there).The Chromecast is easy to set up and use, and is unobtrusive. It is also considerably cheaper than the Roku 3, and although I don't want to generalize, if you have a device capable of controlling the Chromecast, the price difference probably isn't going to be a deal breaker for you.For me, the Roku 3 is the real winner.
